articles.title: French protesters chant against inflation and police
articles.excerpt: Protesters waved the French flag from the top of a Paris statue on Saturday, as demonstrators across France vented a…
articles.fullText:
Protesters waved the French flag from the top of a Paris statue on Saturday, as demonstrators across France vented a broad range of frustrations from the rising cost of living to opposition to a new police bill.

The European Union's second largest economy has been gripped by high-school blockades and demonstrations demanding better wages for more than a month, before presidential elections next year to replace Emmanuel Macron.

Some of the largely peaceful rallies have seen fringe violence, as well as accusations of police brutality, including against young teenagers.

"No justice, no peace," a protester shouted into a megaphone on the capital's Republique square on Saturday afternoon, as people took to the streets for the fifth Saturday in a row.

Yellow Vest movement member Benjamin Ball was among several thousands of protesters in Paris, who also included students, unions and rights activists.

"The government has only given us crumbs, and we want the whole bakery," he said.

Adrien, a 20-year-old cello player who came as part of a volunteer orchestra, said the focus of the day was a new bill in parliament to give police who use their weapons a presumption of legitimate self-defence.

"We're scared when we come to a protest, and this will only make us even more afraid if their impunity is strengthened," he said, after tear gas fell on a similar group of protesting musicians last month.

Backers of the new police bill -- including the far-right party of leading presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen -- say a new law is necessary to avoid law enforcement officers being automatically suspected of using disproportionate force.

Activists argue it would amount to a "licence to kill".

They say it would make holding security forces accountable even harder in a country where cases of alleged police brutality rarely reach a criminal court.

Lawyers last week said police violence at recent protests that led to "mutilations" including hand, foot and eye injuries.

Around 146,000 people took part in demonstrations across France on Saturday last week, according to authorities, far lower numbers than on previous weekends.

The largest protests in recent weeks occurred during a union-led strike on Thursday last week, when more than half a million people took to the streets nationwide, according to official figures.

Unions have called for a new day of strikes on Tuesday, after rejecting a government promise to increase the minimum wage by 0.6 percent as "crumbs".

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: China and US hold first trade council meeting
articles.excerpt: China and the United States held the first meeting of the trade council under the China-US economic and trade consultation…
articles.fullText:
China and the United States held the first meeting of the trade council under the China-US economic and trade consultation mechanism via video link on Friday, China's Ministry of Commerce said on Saturday.

Guided by the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, the meeting focused on implementing the outcomes of previous rounds of bilateral economic and trade consultations.

The two sides had a candid, in-depth and constructive exchange on tariffs, the reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement covering about US$30 billion worth of each other's goods, agricultural trade and other issues of mutual concern.

Both sides will continue to strengthen communication through the trade council, work to resolve their respective economic and trade concerns, further expand cooperation and shorten the list of issues, so as to help build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity, the ministry noted.

In May, China and the United States agreed to establish a trade council to address their respective concerns in trade cooperation.

The two sides held the eighth round of their economic and trade consultations in New York and Washington DC from September 20 to 23. During the consultations, they agreed to reduce tariffs on about US$30 billion worth of goods imported from each other on a reciprocal basis, with tariffs on around 90 percent of the covered products to be lowered to most-favored-nation rates. (Xinhua)

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: Svitolina makes WTA Finals semis by beating Sabalenka
articles.excerpt: Elina Svitolina overcame Aryna Sabalenka 6-3, 3-6, 6-1 to reach the semifinals of the WTA Finals on Friday, winning on…
articles.fullText:
Elina Svitolina overcame Aryna Sabalenka 6-3, 3-6, 6-1 to reach the semifinals of the WTA Finals on Friday, winning on her fourth match point.

Both players had more errors than winners. Svitolina hit 21 winners, made 24 errors and won six of eight break points in beating Sabalenka for the first time in six years and just the second in their eight career meetings.

“She gave me a few chances here and there so I could find my shots,” said Svitolina, who won the finals in 2018, was runner-up in 2019 and then didn't qualify again until this year.

Sabalenka, who was runner-up last year, rallied to take the second set and was up an early break in the third before coming undone with 35 errors. Her trademark frustration took over, as she talked to herself, gestured, shook her head and appeared disgusted. She didn't speak to the media afterward.

Svitolina will face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova in the semifinals on Saturday at Indian Wells Tennis Garden. Svitolina became a first-time mother four years ago.

“I want my daughter to see me win tournaments,” she said.

Mirra Andreeva won 12 of the final 13 games to cruise past her frequent doubles partner Diana Shnaider 6-2, 6-1 and will play Jessica Pegula in the other semifinal. The Russian teenager dropped just 11 games total in winning group two with a 3-0 record.

Shnaider, the second alternate, was a late replacement for Karolina Muchova, who withdrew with a gastrointestinal illness. Shnaider made her WTA Finals debut in singles after qualifying in doubles last year with fellow Russian Andreeva. They went 0-3 in round-robin play a year ago.

Muchova, a Wimbledon finalist this year, already lost her first two matches and could not have advanced to the semifinals even if she had played on Friday.

She is the second withdrawal of the eight-day, US$10 million event. Top-ranked Elena Rybakina dropped out before the tournament began almost a week ago, citing a viral illness and exhaustion. (AP)

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: Over a dozen HK flights affected by US groundstop
articles.excerpt: Two Hong Kong-bound flights from the US were cancelled and seven others were delayed, according to the Airport Authority Hong…
articles.fullText:
Two Hong Kong-bound flights from the US were cancelled and seven others were delayed, according to the Airport Authority Hong Kong, after US aviation officials issued a temporary nationwide ground stop.

For flights from Hong Kong to the US, two were cancelled, and six were delayed.

The ground stop lasted around four hours and was lifted at 8.15pm Eastern Time, or 9.15am on Saturday Hong Kong time.

Flight delays between the US and Hong Kong are expected to last till Sunday, with the Airport Authority urging passengers to pay attention to the latest announcements from airlines.

The incident marked only the second time such an alert had been issued in US airspace - which is among the busiest in the world - since the 9/11 attacks.

US officials have dismissed reports of a potential cyberattack.

Instead, they are blaming the air traffic communication glitch on the ageing equipment used for air traffic control.

A total of 33 flights were scheduled between Hong Kong and the United States for the day.

The city's flagship carrier said it has arranged accommodation for affected passengers and will continue to closely monitor the situation.

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: Few smooth operators for rock hall of fame's big night
articles.excerpt: Billy Idol, Oasis, Wu-Tang Clan, Phil Collins, Sade, Queen Latifah, Iron Maiden, Joy Division/New Order and the late Luther Vandross…
articles.fullText:
Billy Idol, Oasis, Wu-Tang Clan, Phil Collins, Sade, Queen Latifah, Iron Maiden, Joy Division/New Order and the late Luther Vandross will be inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame on Saturday.

But the list of who will show up and perform is getting shorter daily and looking awfully thin, and it's difficult to know what the ceremony will look like with so many artists not playing the sets that define the show.

Sade - the group whose sensual, captivating rhythms have endured as fan favorites for decades with hits including "Smooth Operator" and "No Ordinary Love" - said they were bowing out in a statement on their website.

"Sorry we can't be there in person to celebrate with the other artists. Please know that our absence takes nothing away from how much this recognition means to us," said the group, fronted by the singer Sade Adu.

Britpop's one-time feuding brothers Liam and Noel Gallagher of Oasis - who recently announced a 2027 world tour - also declined to make the trip.

The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame may make a few announcements later this week about who is inducting the new members and who may perform their songs in their place, although organisers like to keep much of the show a surprise.

For the second straight year, the ceremony that moves between Cleveland, New York and Los Angeles will be held at the Peacock Theater in downtown LA. After two years of streaming it live, the Rock Hall is returning to its previous model, where the public won't see it until an edited version airs on ABC and Disney+ in December.

The list of 2026 honourees also includes MC Lyte, Celia Cruz , Fela Kuti and Gram Parsons, along with music producers Rick Rubin, Linda Creed, Arif Mardin and Jimmy Miller and variety show host Ed Sullivan.

Billy Idol, who toured the US in summer and had a residency in Las Vegas, plans to play and says he’s going to “bring it” when he does.

Wu-Tang Clan, which toured together just last year on what was billed as a farewell tour, may play after getting into the hall with their first nomination. (AP/AFP)

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: No government systems hit by Microsoft outage
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong has so far received no reports of government systems being affected by Friday’s disruption to Microsoft services. In…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong has so far received no reports of government systems being affected by Friday’s disruption to Microsoft services.

In response to enquiries, the Digital Policy Office said it was highly concerned about the software system failure, which disrupted services including Outlook and Teams for more than 24 hours.

The office said it had not yet received reports of government department systems being affected and would continue to monitor the situation closely while providing support and advice to departments.

On whether Hong Kong’s critical infrastructure had been affected, the Security Bureau said the government had drawn on the experience of the mainland and other jurisdictions.

Taking into account Hong Kong’s relevant legal requirements and carefully considering appropriate arrangements for information disclosure, the government – for security reasons – will not publicly disclose the list of critical infrastructure operators or related details.

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: Woman injured in Ngau Tau Kok traffic incident
articles.excerpt: An 82-year-old woman has been hospitalised in an unconscious state after being hit by a light goods vehicle in Ngau…
articles.fullText:
An 82-year-old woman has been hospitalised in an unconscious state after being hit by a light goods vehicle in Ngau Tau Kok around noon on Saturday.

The 40-year-old driver was arrested on suspicion of dangerous driving.

Police said the driver was travelling along Tung Ming Street when he is alleged to have struck the woman as she was crossing at the junction with Ngau Tau Kok Road.

Officers said the woman suffered head injuries and was taken to Queen Elizabeth Hospital.

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: HK 'needs to step up act on AI laws on porn and scams'
articles.excerpt: Lawmakers have called on the government to tighten artificial intelligence regulations after the city ranked just 50th out of 70…
articles.fullText:
Lawmakers have called on the government to tighten artificial intelligence regulations after the city ranked just 50th out of 70 economies for AI governance in a new global index.

In terms of competitiveness, the Switzerland-based International Institute for Management Development's first-ever World Digital and AI Ranking report also ranked the SAR as 11th overall and fourth in Asia, behind Singapore and the Chinese mainland with the United States topping the list.

Speaking on a radio show on Saturday, lawmaker Johnny Ng said while the city had performed well in talent and infrastructure, it lagged behind on governance.

"It's not that we don't have laws. We have guidelines," he said.

"But when it comes to certain areas, for example, how we protect young people from pornography or scams, we need to do a little more."

Speaking on the same show, fellow lawmaker Simon Lee said current regulations were not enough.

He said the city should consider rolling out AI legislation in phases, with priority placed on monitoring of deepfakes and high-risk AI systems.

In his September 2026 Policy Address, Chief Executive John Lee said the city was looking at instituting legislation to regulate deepfakes and combat AI-enabled crime.

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: US planes taking off as full resumption 'to take time'
articles.excerpt: Flights in the United States have been resuming on Saturday after being grounded for several hours due to a major…
articles.fullText:
Flights in the United States have been resuming on Saturday after being grounded for several hours due to a major communications outage, though authorities said returning to normal operations would take time.

The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to US$50 billion late on Friday after the communications issue forced a nationwide groundstop that halted thousands of flights.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and the White House had earlier asked for US$30.1 billion to upgrade the United States' aging airports and air traffic control system.

The outage sparked widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before departure by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events.

The incident marked only the second time such an alert had been issued in US airspace – among the busiest in the world – since the 9/11 attacks.

The ground stop lasted around four hours and was lifted at 8.15pm Eastern Time, or 9.15am on Saturday Hong Kong time.

Federal Aviation Administration officials reopened the airspace on Friday night "after restoring full functionality" at air traffic control facilities, according to Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy.

"It will take us time [to] resume normal operations... Our top priority is the safety of you and your family when you fly," he said.

Administration officials blamed the incident on telecommunications issues with decades-old equipment, adding there was no evidence of foul play.

"This is a legacy system problem," Duffy said. "We have old, old switches, old routers.

"We use 1980s little copper lines. It's an old system that went down, and went down everywhere. It got overloaded."

As the ground stop was lifted, he repeated his plea.

"I'm going to say it a million times: the Congress has to give the resources to the president so he can finish this bill," he said.

There were almost 6,000 flights canceled, including some international routes, according to FlightAware, a tracking platform.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stressed there was no evidence of any hostile action on Friday.

"We've seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack or [AI] attack," he said.

He also ruled out any connection with the outage that affected Microsoft this week, knocking email systems offline for millions of users, public services and businesses worldwide. (AFP)

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: MTR pledges no compromise on Northern Link safety
articles.excerpt: MTR Corporation chief executive Jeny Yeung said the quality and safety standards of the Northern Link line that it is…
articles.fullText:
MTR Corporation chief executive Jeny Yeung said the quality and safety standards of the Northern Link line that it is building will not be compromised despite a significantly reduced cost forecast.

Her remarks came after the government gave the green light to the second phase of the project this week, revealing that the entire railway link is expected to cost about HK$86.2 billion - around 28 percent lower than initial estimates as a result of a shortened construction period and cost-saving measures.

Speaking on a television programme aired on Saturday, Yeung also said the rail operator was not concerned about the project going over budget.

"We shall work very hard to control costs when working on the project," she said.

"In addition, we will also utilise more technology and, in the process, use as much innovative thinking as possible.

"Like I just said, we shall jointly build part one and part two of the railway link, and the approach will also benefit from innovative thinking."

Yeung added that the Northern Link would likely adopt equipment aligned with mainland railway standards to enable greater procurement flexibility, following the promulgation of the Hong Kong Railway Standards in February, which for the first time systematically integrate mainland standards alongside international frameworks.

Under the project agreement signed on Tuesday, the government also granted eight sites along the Northern Link to the rail operator for residential and commercial development.

Yeung said not all of the sites are expected to be put out for market tender by 2034, when both the main line and the spur line are scheduled to be commissioned simultaneously. Sites close to nearly completed stations, such as Kwu Tung, will be prioritised for development, she added.

Overall, the corporation is currently working on seven separate projects, she said, predicting that the three-year period starting from 2029 will mark its peak construction phase.

Regarding a recent incident in which around 30 pillars at the platform level of the under-construction Tung Chung West Station were found to be substandard, Yeung said the company was still aiming to meet the original commissioning timeline of December 2029.

Asked why there was a one-month gap between the MTR's discovery of the issue and its public announcement in November, she stressed that staff had ordered the contractor to suspend work immediately after spotting suspected irregularities during routine inspections.

Staff subsequently spent time inspecting other columns and uncovered further issues, she explained.

Yeung went on to say that the MTR was taking the irregularities seriously and pledged to update the public as more details came to light.

Edited by Azam Khan

articles.title: 12 held in crackdown on illegal cross-border car hires
articles.excerpt: Police have arrested 12 drivers suspected of providing illegal cross-border hire cars over the past two weeks, Police Commissioner Joe…
articles.fullText:
Police have arrested 12 drivers suspected of providing illegal cross-border hire cars over the past two weeks, Police Commissioner Joe Chow said.

Speaking after a police passing-out parade, he said the arrests were part of a series of operations targeting unlicensed cross-border hire cars, commonly known as "white licence" cars, including one near Kai Tak, where a large concert was being held.

Chow said officers made no arrests on Friday night but towed away a modified seven-seater vehicle.

Police, he said, had also published short promotional videos on social media urging tourists and locals not to use cross-border white licence cars.

He said the force would continue similar operations in the coming nights and around other large events.

Asked whether the police would work with mainland departments to tighten licensing criteria, Chow said police had long maintained close contact with different departments across the border.

"We will continue to maintain coordination and contact with them in all aspects in the hope of further improving the situation," he said.

Edited by Robert Kemp

Following an investigation, officers arrested the three suspects, aged between 13 and 15, in Eastern and Sham Shui Po on Friday.

articles.title: Stiffer proxy checks set for flat owners' votes
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong is putting in place a verification regime for proxy votes at property owners’ corporation meetings, Secretary for Home…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong is putting in place a verification regime for proxy votes at property owners’ corporation meetings, Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak said on Saturday.

Checks requiring both parties to sign and declare are, she said, "more effective" than a prescribed cap on the number of proxy votes a flat owner's representative can hold.

Speaking on an RTHK radio programme, Mak said the government has received 550 written submissions from a month-long public consultation on proposed amendments to the Building Management Ordinance.

The submissions, she pointed out, broadly supported clearer thresholds for major maintenance works and stronger proxy requirements but raised practical concerns.

Mak said half of the submissions opposed the proposed cap on how many proxy votes one person may hold, citing the difficulty of applying a numerical limit once forms are sealed in a box and opened collectively.

Instead, she said, both parties would have to sign off on the forms and leave contact details, with the owner declaring they know about the meeting and agenda, and the representative declaring they know the person authorising the proxy representation is the genuine owner of the property.

“Verification is more effective than a prescribed cap," Mak said.

"Many owners and industry friends said verification is better able than a prescribed cap to ensure the proxy system is not abused."

Mak said the biggest difficulty in the past was proving whether a person knew the owner was genuine or bogus and had actually authorised the proxy, which was why the government would be requiring both parties to sign.

On major maintenance works, she said the statutory quorum – the 10 percent attendance needed for an owners’ meeting to proceed – will stay unchanged.

However, in-person voting thresholds will be tiered, with each set at the lower of the percentage or the owner count: five percent or 100 owners where the apportioned cost exceeds HK$30,000 per unit; eight percent or 150 owners where it exceeds HK$80,000; and 10 percent or 200 owners where it exceeds HK$120,000.

The tiered thresholds, Mak said, are intended to encourage more owners to vote as the apportioned cost rises and to play a more active role in building management and maintenance works.

She added that proxy votes cannot be used to meet those in-person thresholds.

A briefing session, Mak said, must be held seven days before the owners’ meeting, after tender results and analysis are available.

"If no briefing session is held, under the law they will not be allowed to vote on the major maintenance works at the subsequent owners’ meeting," she said.

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: Poch says Man Utd job was 'most difficult decision'
articles.excerpt: Mauricio Pochettino said leaving his role as USA boss to take charge of Manchester United was "one of the most…
articles.fullText:
Mauricio Pochettino said leaving his role as USA boss to take charge of Manchester United was "one of the most difficult" decisions of his career as he prepares for one of football's toughest jobs.

The 54-year-old Argentine fought back tears on Friday as he bade an emotional farewell to US football, hours after the Premier League giants announced he would replace the sacked Michael Carrick.

The former Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea boss will take up his new position on November 18, with a monumental task ahead of him.

United have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years and are languishing in the Premier League relegation zone during the current international break.

Pochettino is understood to have signed a two-and-a-half-year deal at Old Trafford, taking him through to the end of the 2028/29 season.

"We learned a lot from you all, from this amazing country," Pochettino said in Fayetteville, Georgia. "I think this was one of the most difficult decisions of [my] career."

Pochettino, who led the USA to the last 16 at this year's World Cup, will oversee back-to-back Concacaf Nations League matches against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday before leaving for England.

He said he had not considered a possible return to the Premier League when he signed a contract extension with US Soccer in August, but added the opportunity to join United was too good to turn down.

"I never said I wanted to go back in the Premier League," he said. "Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives."

US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson said Pochettino had left a lasting legacy through his "leadership, professionalism and commitment to our players and culture".

The federation is reportedly set to receive around US$10 million in compensation, plus more to cover the departure of Pochettino's coaching staff.

United said in a statement that Pochettino was "renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players".

"Pochettino has consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues," the club added.

The 20-time English champions are one of the giants of world football but have largely been also-rans since Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Pochettino is the eighth permanent manager tasked with returning the Red Devils to former glories.

He started his Premier League managerial career with Southampton before joining Tottenham, where he never finished lower than fifth during his five full seasons in charge and also reached the 2019 Champions League final.

Pochettino claimed the first trophies of his managerial career with PSG, collecting the 2021 French Cup and 2022 Ligue 1 title, but did not see out his contract in Paris.

He returned to the dugout at Chelsea in 2023 but only lasted one season.

The former Argentina defender, who has been linked with the United job on several previous occasions, faces a baptism of fire at the home of fierce rivals Liverpool on November 22.

He must unite a club that is deeply divided on and off the pitch.

United captain Bruno Fernandes was dropped last month after he criticised Carrick's tactics and Lisandro Martinez took a public swipe at the United hierarchy over a lack of investment.

Angry fans vented their frustration at the club's ownership following the sacking of the popular Carrick, who won multiple trophies as a player.

Despite fierce and persistent protests over two decades, the US-based Glazer family still hold a majority stake in United, which Malcolm Glazer bought via a leveraged takeover in 2005, saddling the club with huge debts.

Any hopes the arrival of British billionaire Jim Ratcliffe as a minority owner in 2024 would signal a new dawn have since faded.

Carrick issued an emotional statement Friday wishing United "nothing but success", adding that his love for the club "never dies". (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: SpaceX faces Starship first as booster catch aborted
articles.excerpt: Elon Musk's SpaceX has aborted the recovery of the booster for the latest flight of the world's biggest and most…
articles.fullText:
Elon Musk's SpaceX has aborted the recovery of the booster for the latest flight of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, the Starship, but insisted it could yet "catch" the spaceship, which would be a first.

The 124-metre rocket roared into the sky from Starbase in southern Texas for its 15th test flight on Friday, but minutes later, the planned landmark nature of the mission went awry.

After lift-off and the mid-air separation of the two stages, a technical problem forced the company to abandon plans to recover the booster, dubbed Super Heavy, allowing it to instead splash down in the Gulf of Mexico.

The spacecraft itself entered its orbit of the Earth, and SpaceX will attempt to recover it on Saturday after 22 hours of spaceflight.

Successful recoveries of both Starship components would have marked a significant milestone in the space industry's decades-long pursuit of fully reusable rocket systems that can drastically reduce mission costs and make frequent launches possible.

The company had caught the booster on three previous occasions, with the first stage descending vertically back to the launch site shortly after blastoff and nestling into mechanical "chopstick" arms.

If SpaceX can capture the spacecraft that gives the rocket system its name, it will be a groundbreaking moment in the development of the vessel, some versions of which are designed to launch internet satellites and data centres into orbit.

Other iterations will be made to ferry people to the Moon and Mars.

A spacecraft that can be fully reused is the "Holy Grail" of the space industry, said Clayton Swope, an aerospace expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

"No one's really been able to do that so far," he said. "People have been trying to do that since the [Nasa] space shuttle. But the space shuttle ended up being kind of a compromise because a lot of the vehicle wasn't reusable."

Recovering an upper stage involves an extraordinary amount of precision, said Kathleen Curlee, a senior analyst at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

"Getting Starship off the ground is an engineering achievement in and of itself; catching the upper stage involves millions of moving parts that all have to go right for a successful capture," she said.

The spaceship will be falling much faster and from a much higher altitude than the booster, with the vessel forced to withstand the extreme heat of reentering Earth's atmosphere.

The Starship project has been plagued by years-long delays as SpaceX grapples with novel engineering challenges – even as Nasa is counting on the spaceship to serve as a lunar lander for its Artemis program.

Other technical challenges include transferring fuel to Starship in orbit – a requirement for any journey to the Moon or Mars.

Following SpaceX's high-profile stock market debut in June that raised about US$85.7 billion, the company carried out the first orbital flight of Starship in September, though the mission was cut short due to an engine issue.

Starship has deployed 26 satellites into Musk's Starlink satellite internet constellation that has become a major revenue stream for SpaceX.

It is in the process of attempting to circle the planet 14 times, before returning 22 hours later and – SpaceX hopes – descending safely into the chopstick arms.

SpaceX has said it would proceed with these manoeuvres only if conditions are optimal, and in the past has made last-minute changes to test flights under Musk's "fail fast" strategy of learning through crashes, explosions and other mishaps. (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: US ends nationwide grounding of flights
articles.excerpt: The US Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by…
articles.fullText:
The US Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems.

The green light for resumption came after the FAA had grounded all flights nationwide on Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted. Officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centres.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the September 11, 2001, attacks.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the problem to a telecommunications outage and said there was no indication yet of a nefarious act. The consequences were profound, disrupting thousands of planned flights through at least late Friday night and upending travel plans for passengers.

“It’s frustrating. This certainly sounds like it’s going to be more than the usual run-of-the-mill delay. I look forward to finding out why,” said Jeff Dubner, a Washington attorney whose Alaska Airlines flight home from Los Angeles was already half an hour late and taxiing to the runway when the plane came to a halt.

The FAA was investigating a communication issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centres that direct planes en route between airports nationwide, said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

International flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Mullin, with some seen taking off Friday evening. Meanwhile, some flights within Alaska and Hawaii were not impacted, Alaska Airlines said.

Mullin said at the White House that there was no indication yet that “this was a nefarious attack against us. It's just a telecommunications outage as of right now.”

“Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying,” he said.

At least 827 flights have been diverted so far as a result. As of 7.05pm EST, 8.05am on Saturday Hong Kong time, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

The airports where many of the flights ended up being diverted included Washington Dulles International, Los Angeles International, Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International and Nashville International.

Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the United States after 4pm EST, raising the likelihood of more cancellations and flight diversions.

United Airlines and American Airlines said flights already in the air will continue.

“It will be all hands on deck across American to get customers on their way as soon as possible when the FAA lifts this nationwide ground stop,” American said in a statement on the social platform X.

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.

Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.

FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it is prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.

US airlines move about 61,000 tonnes of goods – from letters to packages – to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

The government has been working to overhaul outdated technology

There is no timeline for restarting flights. Mullin said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, DC, and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centres.

The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved US$12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fibre optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.

But much work remains. Duffy has said that another US$30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.” (AP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: US markets end lower as Nvidia casts a pall
articles.excerpt: A pullback in big AI-focused companies weighed on the market, capping a turbulent week on Wall Street. The S&P 500…
articles.fullText:
A pullback in big AI-focused companies weighed on the market, capping a turbulent week on Wall Street.

The S&P 500 fell 0.4 percent, but managed to post a 2.5 percent gain for the week.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average recovered from an early slide and eked out a 0.1 percent gain. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.9 percent, but also notched its first weekly gain in five weeks.

The S&P 500 fell 30.73 points to 7,561.67, the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 50.46 points to 52,347.55, and the Nasdaq lost 229.82 points to close at 25,136.27.

The major indexes have been shaky this week as some of the biggest AI companies pushed and pulled the market.

The market remained unsteady a day after the AI industry was rocked by the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be its interim CEO. The ensuing fallout cost Nvidia’s market cap more than US$600 billion this week.

Nvidia fell 2 percent. Broadcom fell 4.8 percent and Advanced Micro Devices lost 8.8 percent.

Nvidia in particular has been slipping for weeks amid wider concerns about a potential slowdown for the industry.

“Nvidia's pullback serves as a reminder of the concentration risk embedded in a market where a small number of mega-cap technology stocks have driven an outsized share of returns,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note.

Microsoft rose 0.2 percent, despite suffering a global outage for its web services that disrupted email accounts and other applications.

A report on Friday showed that wholesale inflation cooled slightly last month, but remains high . The report measures inflation experienced by businesses, before it can reach consumers. Inflation at the consumer level remains stubbornly high at well above 3 percent. That's higher than the Fed's preferred target of 2 percent.

The latest wholesale inflation report also showed food prices and other costs gaining ground, despite some easing for energy costs.

“That suggests inflation is working its way into the broader economy rather than remaining concentrated in the original areas of price pressure,” said Chris Osmond, chief investment officer for Fifth Third Wealth Advisors, in a research note. “If that continues, it becomes much harder for the Fed to simply look through inflation as temporary.”

The central bank held rates steady at its last meeting, following a previous rate hike. The latest hot updates on inflation have prompted economists to overwhelmingly expect a rate hike at the upcoming December meeting, with another hike likely to follow in January. (AP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: All US flights halted by national ground stop order
articles.excerpt: The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide on Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control…
articles.fullText:
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide on Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centres.

The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said there is a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centres that direct planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians are investigating. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 , when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved US$12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fibre optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.

But much work remains. Duffy has said that another US$30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.”

Friday’s ground stop was different than the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: UN head urges climate summit to act now
articles.excerpt: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday called for an "immediate and drastic reduction" in greenhouse gas emissions, as divisions over…
articles.fullText:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday called for an "immediate and drastic reduction" in greenhouse gas emissions, as divisions over fossil fuels dominated the first week of COP31 climate talks in Turkey.

Big fossil fuel producers and consumers at the talks are resisting any deal that would specify firm new targets or a shift away from oil, gas and coal, observers said as the first week of talks drew to a close.

That poses a challenge for summit host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia, which have another week to land the kind of ambitious agreement climate advocates such as Guterres say is needed.

"The central question is in the hands of member states, particularly the big emitters. They must recognise the need for an immediate and drastic reduction in emissions to keep the 1.5 goal still possible by the end of the century," he said, referring to the warming limit countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement.

A UN report last month found the world is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming threshold, a limit scientists say should prevent the worst effects of climate change.

As temperatures have risen, this year has been marked by extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood that killed more than 1,450 people. Thousands more are still missing.

Major oil producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have traditionally resisted language constraining fossil fuels, while large developing economies such as India have opposed measures they say could limit their development and energy choices, a dynamic that has compromised the outcomes of past deals.

The world’s biggest oil consumer, the United States, meanwhile, has skipped the talks for the second year in a row under US President Donald Trump, who has called global warming a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.

"We must confront the disproportionate influence of the fossil fuel lobby. The future of our planet cannot be negotiated on the terms of those profiting from its destruction," said Guterres, who is leaving his job at the end of December after two five-year terms.

"But I remain hopeful. I've also seen something extraordinary over these 10 years. Renewable energy has moved from the margins to the mainstream. The economics have changed. The technology has advanced. A cleaner, safer, and more secure energy future is in our hands. The question is whether we have the courage and speed to reach for it."

Cop31 host Turkey is striving to place a proposal to expand global electrification at the centre of an eventual deal, saying the plan will lead to emissions cuts by speeding the shift away from fossil fuel-powered cars, boilers and other equipment.

The proposal does not require the increased electricity use to come from renewable sources, although some countries, including last year’s Cop host Brazil, are advocating for progress on a plan to require countries to more clearly map out their transition away from fossil fuels.

Katrine Petersen, an observer for the non-governmental organisation E3G, said whether those measures survive the talks depends on conversations in the days to come.

"We've also heard quite clearly from countries like India, the G77, that they don't want any firm targets. They don't want any kind of technology or fuel-specific language," she said. "(These are) the kind of consistent and ongoing divides that we've seen from those different parties before."

Representatives from India, Saudi Arabia and Russia did not immediately comment.

Diana Acconcia, head of the EU delegation, said Europe backed the electrification goal.

"Electrification is, in a way, an inclusive agenda because it is non-prescriptive in a way on how the electrification is achieved," she said. "Of course, for the European Union electrification is to be achieved by clean sources of energy."

The Australian team, which is leading negotiations under a split presidency arrangement, spent the first few days of the summit gathering views on what should be included in a political text agreed by consensus that will be followed by all the negotiated technical points.

Australia is taking further submissions from countries until Saturday night, with a view to formulating a draft text early next week. (Reuters)

Edited by Robert Kemp

The Transport Department today alerted the public to fraudulent vehicle airbag safety recall messages purporting to be from the department. The case will be referred to Police for follow-up.

The department clarified that it has no connection with the fraudulent letters or messages making unauthorised use of its name. At present, it only sets out safety recall information provided by authorised dealers of registered vehicle manufacturers on its website .

The department does not issue letters to inform individual vehicle owners of safety recalls for their vehicles. Members of the public should verify information to avoid falling into scam traps and contact the relevant authorised agents or dealers directly for enquiries.

articles.title: In Peru, Pope Leo makes emotional homecoming
articles.excerpt: Pope Leo XIV returned on Friday to his beloved former diocese of Chiclayo, an emotional homecoming that underscored his love…
articles.fullText:
Pope Leo XIV returned on Friday to his beloved former diocese of Chiclayo, an emotional homecoming that underscored his love for his Peruvian flock and their pride that their shepherd now runs the Catholic Church.

The pope's Latam charter touched down at Chiclayo’s airport on the Pacific coast. On the side of the aircraft was the message that has followed Leo wherever he has gone in Peru: #LeonXIVvuelaaCasa (Leon XIV flies home).

Chiclayo, population 700,000, is the commercial hub of Peru’s northern Pacific coast. But much of the world heard about it on the night of Leo’s election, May 8, 2025, when he gave Chiclayo a shoutout, in Spanish, from the loggia of St. Peter’s Basilica.

And on Friday, Chiclayo was welcoming its former shepherd home.

“I’m so glad he’s returning,” said Rolando Antonio Mendoza, who was selling posters bearing the pope's image in front of the cathedral where Leo used to celebrate Mass.

“Even though he’s now Pope Leo XIV, he hasn’t forgotten about his homeland.”

Church organisers say as many as a million people could turn out for Leo’s first big Mass in Peru, being held on Friday morning on a massive field outside Chiclayo.

The former Robert Prevost spent two decades as a missionary priest and bishop in Peru and credits the place and its people with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Pope Francis sent the Chicago-born Augustinian to take over as bishop of Chiclayo in 2014 and he stayed until Francis summoned him to Rome in 2023 to run the Vatican's bishops' office.

In hindsight, the 2023 transfer to Rome signalled that Francis saw in Prevost a potential successor, since the job is one of the most important in the church and would give Prevost the Vatican experience that many consider necessary to be a viable contender for the papacy.

But Prevost's heart is in Chiclayo, where he remains beloved for championing social justice issues and for his closeness to the people, especially poor people, during times of crisis. And he had quite a few during his tenure: Covid-19, devastating floods and a surge of Venezuelan migrants as the humanitarian situation worsened there in 2018.

“Chiclayo is a party,” said Rocio Zena, who remembered how Prevost helped her when she lost her family home in the 2023 floods. “We’re overjoyed to welcome the Holy Father with so much faith. He arrives, no longer as Prevost but as Leo XIV. And he’s coming home.”

In town, the El Trebol restaurant proudly calls itself the restaurant of the pope and his image is displayed in framed photos of Prevost riding a horse, wading through the mud in rubber boots and celebrating his birthday with a cake.

A sign on his favorite table – No. 3 – with a view of the cathedral, reads: “mesa bendita” – Spanish for blessed table. Like many other places around the city, the restaurant sells “Papaletas” or “Pop(e)sicles" with Leo's image in white chocolate.

Ever since Leo touched down on Peruvian soil on Wednesday, the world has seen a very different pope.

Normally reserved and placid, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed at turns positively giddy and overwhelmed with emotion to the point of tears.

That was certainly the case on Thursday night when some 60,000 young Peruvians sang for him in the Lima stadium. It was also the case when he sang the national anthem at the presidential palace upon his arrival on Wednesday.

Leo has also sung along with popular songs and hymns, tapping his fingers to the beat on an armchair.

On other occasions, he has shown himself so relaxed and comfortable as to joke about his health. Speaking to Peruvian bishops, he joked about how some “doubting Thomases” didn’t think he’d make it because of his recent lung cancer surgery.

After the Mass, Leo's other main events of the day include a meeting with Chiclayo clergy and seminarians and a speech to the Catholic university where he served as chancellor during his years as bishop.

The university is named for the 16th-century first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius de Mogrovejo. (AP)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Pochettino named Man United manager
articles.excerpt: Mauricio Pochettino was named Manchester United's new manager on Friday, tasked with reviving the struggling giants following the dismissal of…
articles.fullText:
Mauricio Pochettino was named Manchester United's new manager on Friday, tasked with reviving the struggling giants following the dismissal of Michael Carrick.

The Red Devils issued a statement saying the USA coach, who has extensive experience in the Premier League, would take charge from November 18 following two matches against Haiti.

The 54-year-old is understood to have signed a two-and-a-half-year deal at Old Trafford, taking him through to the end of the 2028/29 season.

"The club has reached an agreement with the US soccer federation for Mauricio and his staff to be released after the conclusion of their responsibilities with the US men's national team," United said.

"The Argentinian is renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players.

"Pochettino has consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues."

Pochettino, who led the United States to the last-16 of the World Cup on home soil earlier this year, said in a statement released by US Soccer that the job with the national team had been "one of the greatest honours of my career".

"We are so grateful to the players for their commitment, to the fans for their belief, and to the federation for always supporting our staff and creating the opportunities to impact the culture of soccer in this great country," he added.

US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson said Pochettino had left a lasting mark on football in the United States through his "leadership, professionalism and commitment to our players and culture".

The federation is reportedly set to receive US$10 million in compensation for him, plus a further US$2 million for the departure of his coaching staff.

Pochettino has previously managed Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea in England, and also coached Paris Saint-Germain.

He never finished lower than fifth in the Premier League during his five seasons at Tottenham.

But despite his relative success at Spurs, Pochettino failed to win silverware and was dismissed in November 2019 – just months after the north London club lost to Liverpool in the Champions League final.

He claimed the first trophies of his managerial career with PSG, collecting the 2021 French Cup and 2022 Ligue 1 title, but did not see out his contract.

Pochettino returned to the dugout at Chelsea in 2023 but lasted a single season, reaching the FA Cup semi-finals and losing in the League Cup final.

Pochettino, who has been linked with the United job on several previous occasions, has a huge task to revive the 20-time English champions, who have endured their worst-ever start to a Premier League campaign.

The Red Devils, next in action at the home of fierce rivals Liverpool on November 22, are in the relegation zone after winning just one of their 10 league matches so far. (AFP)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: The Download: Silicon Valley’s blind spot and Nvidia’s chip-tracking plan
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?

—Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square

The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future. Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers.

Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.

Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think .

Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility

Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China.

The act is drawing renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair. Find out what the proposed tracking measures would involve .

—James O’Donnell

More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials

Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can control robotic limbs and computers, and even “speak.”

The people who volunteer for trials of these devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014.

He’s been working on a set of guidelines for ethical trials to respect participants’ autonomy—and access their own brain data whenever they want.

Read the full story on the push to give volunteers in brain implant trials more rights .

—Jessica Hamzelou

This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

+ Singapore says US failed to help in the spy probe. ( NYT $)
+ The city-state faces growing scrutiny over its chip links to China. ( CNBC )
+ The turmoil at Nvidia puts billions in Chinese AI at risk. ( Reuters $)
+ Taiwan’s “silicon shield” is weakening. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Parents are demanding an AI moratorium in schools
Gemini allegedly encouraged a teenager to plan suicide. ( Ars Technica )
+ Schools are caught in Big Tech’s education experiment. ( New Yorker $)
+ We need smarter AI use in the classroom. ( MIT Technology Review )

They’re targeting Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceXSI. ( AP )

Quote of the day

—Donald Trump shares his succession plan for Nvidia on Truth Social, The Verge reports .

One more thing

COURTESY OF NORWEGIAN PUBLIC ROADS ADMINISTRATION

Inside the world’s deepest and longest subsea road tunnel

—Niall Firth

I’m currently around 1,000 feet beneath the North Sea, in a dark, dank cave. It smells weird. And I’m increasingly aware of the pressure from millions of tons of seawater just above my head.

I’m under the iconic fjords of Norway to visit what will soon become the world’s longest and deepest subsea road tunnel—an exceptional engineering feat that will carry drivers deep beneath the North Sea.

I’m here to understand how you make a 16.6-mile highway that sits 1,280 feet below the sea at its deepest point. And also—at a time when it can feel hard to get anything done—to reassure myself that ambitious engineering is still possible. That we can still make things.

Health authorities said on Friday that a 14-month-old baby girl with severe influenza has died, the third child flu death in Hong Kong this year.

The toddler, who had been in good health, developed a fever and cough in late October and was taken to Tseung Kwan O Hospital after suffering a convulsion.

Her condition deteriorated and she was transferred to the paediatric intensive care unit of United Christian Hospital before passing away on Friday.

In a statement, the Centre for Health Protection said the latest surveillance data showed overall influenza activity has declined but remains above baseline levels.

The centre noted that a cumulative total of 29 severe paediatric influenza cases have been recorded since the start of the current flu season in June.

Apart from the three fatalities, 22 have recovered and been discharged, two are in stable condition and two in critical condition.

Health authorities urged members of the public to promptly receive the seasonal influenza vaccine if they have not yet done so.

articles.excerpt: The government on Friday raised Hong Kong’s economic growth forecast for 2026 to 4.8 percent from the previous forecast of…
articles.fullText:
The government on Friday raised Hong Kong’s economic growth forecast for 2026 to 4.8 percent from the previous forecast of 3.5 to 4.5 percent.

The rise in the full-year GDP forecast came as the SAR saw strong economic expansion in the third quarter while expecting solid growth in the final three months of the year.

Speaking at a press conference, Government Economist Irina Fan said the economy grew by 5.2 percent year-on-year in the third quarter, up from the 4.2 percent growth in the preceding quarter.

She said economic growth in the first nine months of this year reached 5.1 percent over a year earlier – the fastest pace in five years.

“The Hong Kong economy is poised for a strong full-year performance, supported by robust global AI investment and related trade,” Fan said.

“Incoming data on entering the fourth quarter also pointed to sustained growth momentum. Domestic demand should stay resilient.”

She said three drivers of the economy – exports, investment and consumption – continued to grow.

The labour market also stayed broadly stable in the third quarter, with growth in employment earnings over a year earlier, she said.

On inflation, Fan said consumer price inflation has so far been lower than expected.

She noted that while the pass-through of higher oil prices earlier was likely to continue in the coming months, price pressures on other fronts were expected to remain largely contained, so overall inflation should stay moderate.

Fan said the forecast for underlying consumer price inflation rate for 2026 was revised down to 1.9 percent from the previous forecast of 2.5 percent.

The official also said the government will continue to monitor external risks.

“Uncertainties in the external environment persist, including those from geopolitical tensions, US monetary policy, trade protectionist measures, so all these warrant closer monitoring,” she said.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
articles.excerpt: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be…
articles.fullText:
Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”

The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).

Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.”

Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control.

He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it .

The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough .

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.”

In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy.

The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.”

As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.

The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants.

Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data . Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.

The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors.

“It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.”

The guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago , he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.)

Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again.

Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will —an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.

Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that.

Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low . The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference .

“This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.”

This article first appeared in The Checkup,  MIT Technology Review’s  weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first,  sign up here .

articles.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
articles.excerpt: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built…
articles.fullText:
The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda.

Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs .

For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.

What were they thinking?

The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else.

In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die.

Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “ violence and death to our enemies ” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”?

I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand.

There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “ masculine energy ,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats.

In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.”

“Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida , they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones.

Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next.

Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

articles.title: Tech fallout weighs on HK, mainland markets
articles.excerpt: Regional stocks ended mostly lower after a turbulent week dominated by revelations of extramarital affairs involving Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang…

Regional stocks ended mostly lower after a turbulent week dominated by revelations of extramarital affairs involving Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang that culminated in his resignation, in a blow to the global AI boom he helped advance.

In Hong Kong and the mainland, AI model stocks Z.AI and MiniMax Group fell sharply on worries of reduced access to advanced AI chips, while data centre suppliers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink Technology, whose businesses are heavily reliant on US markets, slumped.

Jon Zauderer, Citi's head of specialist sales and a TMT specialist, said competitors such as AMD, Arista and Broadcom could benefit from the Nvidia fallout.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index ended 370 points, or 1.5 percent, lower at 23,637 on turnover of HK$195.86 billion.

The tech index dived 118 points, or three percent, to 3,813 while the China Enterprises Index fell 119 points, or 1.5 percent, to 7,937.

Up north, the Shanghai Composite Index fell 21 points, or 0.59 percent, to close at 3,634, on turnover of 770.6 billion yuan.

The Shenzhen Component Index was 229 points, or 2.05 percent, lower at 10,968 on turnover of 885 billion yuan while the ChiNext Index dived 83 points, or 3.32 percent, to close at 2,426 on turnover of 435.33 billion yuan.
