articles.title: 'SZ, HK should join hands to grow external trade'
articles.excerpt: As Shenzhen's maritime logistics industry has taken off in recent years, a senior official at one of the world's busiest…
articles.fullText:
As Shenzhen's maritime logistics industry has taken off in recent years, a senior official at one of the world's busiest container terminals said Hong Kong still had much to offer as the nation forges closer ties with the world.

Yantian Port, in eastern Shenzhen, is a vital gateway between the nation's manufacturing engine and global markets.

It handles more than one-third of Guangdong's foreign trade and a quarter of the country's container exports to the United States.

According to the Shenzhen municipal government, the deep-water port handled 16.1 million TEUs, or twenty-foot equivalent units, in 2025, representing a 7.1 percent year-on-year increase.

Lawrence Shum, managing director of Yantian, a subsidiary of Hutchison Ports, said the terminal operates nearly 100 international routes on a weekly basis.

Fifty-three of those routes are linked to Apec economies.

"Since the start of this year, we have added 14 new routes to and from Apec economies, further expanding our international network and fostering regional trade," he said.

"According to the customs figures, Shenzhen continues to lead the country in both imports and exports to Apec economies. We even set a record in the first nine months of this year, with a trade value of 3.23 trillion yuan, a 40 percent jump."

Shenzhen is the host of this year's Apec leaders' summit scheduled for November 18 and 19.

Shum explained that Yantian had a unique advantage over other Shenzhen ports when handling shipments from inland regions.

"Yantian houses Shenzhen's only railway that reaches directly into the port area. Through sea‑rail intermodal transport, port services can be extended to inland regions such as the southwest and central areas, making it more convenient for enterprises in Chengdu and Chongqing and bringing them closer to international markets," he said.

Under Shenzhen's 15th Five-Year Plan, Yantian is to strengthen cooperation with Hong Kong's Kwai Tsing Container Terminals.

Shum said six daily vessel trips between the two ports mean cargo can arrive at its destination in about six to eight hours.

"For inland foreign trade enterprises, transportation time can be more stable, more efficient, and more environmentally friendly. Shenzhen and Hong Kong can further tap into inland cargo trade ... and achieve a win‑win for the three regions," Shum said.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: No internet, no advance warning: 11 killed in Myanmar military bombing in Sagaing
articles.excerpt: Civilians in war zones are left vulnerable as Starlink internet becomes scarce after scam center crackdown.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Burmese
It was just before noon on Saturday. Three gyrocopters flew low as they approached Nyaung Pin Lay village. A school and surrounding residential area was bombed. Eleven were killed, including four children.
A resident told RFA that although the local People’s Defense Forces (PDF) received a tip that the Myanmar military would bomb the school, the warning could not reach them in time due to the lack of internet in the village.
“Information that this would be bombed was sent online to everyone. They did inform us,” the Kani Township resident told RFA on the condition of anonymity for security reasons.
“But because there was no Starlink communication, casualties were high as a result. About a month ago in Nat La Po village, when we got the exact location that would be bombed and cleared the area, there were no casualties. That was fortunate. But now, even though we got the location to be bombed, communication was cut off.”
A May 25, 2025, photo shows a Starlink sign at an internet cafe in Demoso, Myanmar.
(AFP) In Myanmar, home to the world’s longest-running civil war, the military-appointed government has cut off phone lines and internet communications in over 40 percent of townships nationwide. Locals, civil society groups, and revolutionary forces tell RFA that they rely on Starlink — acquiring the devices through unofficial and often expensive channels — as a lifeline for information.
In October 2025, SpaceX announced the disabling of over 2,500 Starlink kits in Myanmar to crack down on transnational cyber-scam syndicates operating along the Thai-Myanmar border. Subsequent restrictions by SpaceX on unregistered units bought outside of Myanmar have shut down countless others.
Since June, more than 20 percent of Starlink internet devices used in Myanmar have had their services cut off, according to a report released on Oct. 23 by the group Athan.
Local residents and human rights activists told RFA that this has created a crisis for the survival of civilians in areas of intense civil conflict.
A Myanmar government photo taken on Oct. 20, 2025, shows seized Starlink devices during a raid on the KK Park online scam center in Myawaddy.
(Myanmar Military Information Team via AFP) “The military cutting off phone lines and internet connections from the start was intentionally aimed at concealing human rights violations they commit and restricting people’s freedom of expression,” said Joy, a research director at Athan, a non-profit organization for the Freedom of Expression Movement in Myanmar.
“If Starlink also stops providing services to Myanmar and cuts connections, emergency humanitarian aid, air strike alerts, news regarding military columns, and natural disaster warnings for these local residents will stop immediately.”
According to a report titled “Dead Air” released by Athan on October 23, the communication cut-off directly affects the lives and safety of people in conflict-affected regions as they can no longer receive warnings about airstrikes and military movements, medical aid, or updates on family members’ safety and evacuation routes.
RFA contacted Khaing Khaing Soe, spokesperson for the military-appointed president’s office, regarding when internet and phone lines might be restored. She instead referred RFA to the Ministry of Digital Development and Communications.
Now, not only Starlink devices used by scam operations are being shut down, but Starlink connections used by civilians have also been suspended starting in June this year, with more than 20 percent of devices cut off by October, according to Athan. Consequently, regions like Sagaing, Mandalay, Magway, Rakhine, Kayah State, and other areas experiencing severe conflict were directly affected, Athan’s report states.
RFA contacted SpaceX regarding the impact on civilians in regions where the internet has been cut off, but has not received a response at the time of publication.
“Some of our Starlink devices were disabled. This has caused a lot of trouble for us,” said Aye Myint Aung Aung, Head of the Department of Humanitarian Assistance and Emergency Management under the Mandalay Regional Interim Administrative Council.
“On the other hand, whether it’s our civilians, revolutionary groups, or those leading and operating the administrative mechanism in revolutionary forces, everyone relies on Starlink. As access to information becomes more restricted, limitations on civilian safety also increase. I would define this as a very major challenge for us.”
In Kayah State, Deputy Minister of Defense for the Karenni State Government Khu Daniel told RFA that Starlink connections are being shut down one by one, raising concerns.
“For the public and for the youth currently fighting in battle, it will become a cause for concern,” he said.
A Sept. 17, 2025, photo shows people on a balcony of a building with what appears to be Starlink satellite dishes on the roof in the KK Park complex in Myawaddy, Myanmar.
(Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP) Khun Chit Htoo, who is assisting refugees in the Karenni Region, said that if all Starlink services are shut down, it could have a severe impact on humanitarian aid operations.
“Our current work relies on internet connectivity as well as donors. Since we connect online, we are very concerned,” said Khun Chit Htoo.
“We will face a situation where we can no longer help needy civilians receive the support they really need across all aspects of coordination. If there is no internet line left, I believe we stand to lose a lot because of this single connection.”
While welcoming and supporting the shutdown of Starlink internet lines used by online scam operations to crack down on scam syndicates, 317 civil society organizations issued a statement on July 17 expressing deep concern over potential negative impacts if all Starlink terminals nationwide are shut down.
According to an October 23 report by the Myanmar Internet Project, an organization monitoring internet shutdowns and conflicts, there were 581 military airstrikes that killed at least 353 civilians in the three months from July to September 2026, with 562 of those attacks occurring in areas where internet service was cut off.
Translated by Nayrein Kyaw. Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: China says trade surplus surpassed US$1tn in October
articles.excerpt: China's trade surplus exceeded US$1 trillion for a second year in a row, according to official data released on Tuesday…
articles.fullText:
China's trade surplus exceeded US$1 trillion for a second year in a row, according to official data released on Tuesday.

The nation's foreign trade in goods maintained strong growth momentum in the first 10 months of 2026, with imports posting especially robust gains, according to official data.

Total imports and exports grew 20 percent year on year over the period, accelerating from 18.8 percent in the first nine months, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC).

Exports jumped 35.2 percent year-on-year to US$412.3 billion last month, according to the GAC, while imports in October expanded 41.6 percent to US$307.1 billion.

Between January and October, the country logged a US$1.04 trillion trade surplus, even as the trade surplus narrowed last month to US$105.3 billion from US$133.5 billion in September as imports picked up pace.

Analysts expect China to surpass the record US$1.2 trillion surplus it hit last year.

“We expect Chinese exports to stay strong for the rest of this year, led by electronics and autos,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics.

Meanwhile, exports to the United States surged 32.9 percent last month, the GAC data showed.

The figures come ahead of another meeting between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen next week.

The two have navigated a shaky truce to a trade war since their meeting in October 2025. They also met twice this year.

Beijing on Monday officially announced the extension of a trade truce with Washington due to expire on November 10 by two months, but said last week that expanding its purchases of US farm goods would hinge on the implementation of their agreed reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement.

"The risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will remain elevated in 2027, particularly as Chinese manufacturers continue expanding their presence in overseas markets," said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China.

Greater reliance on exports, however, leaves China's economy increasingly exposed to any slowdown in global demand.

Much of the strength in exports this year has been fuelled by a global push to expand AI infrastructure.

"The outlook for exports depends on how long the AI boom will last," Macquarie analysts wrote.

They expect China's exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before starting to slow from the first quarter of 2027. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: US military surrenders in court fight with WuXi AppTec
articles.excerpt: The US military has removed mainland biotechnology company WuXi AppTec from its list of Chinese military companies, according to a…
articles.fullText:
The US military has removed mainland biotechnology company WuXi AppTec from its list of Chinese military companies, according to a government posting.

The deputy secretary of defence made the determination on Monday in light of a federal court in Washington barring the department from enforcing the designation, the posting said.

The ruling came in a lawsuit WuXi AppTec filed after the Pentagon added it to the list, saying its designation was arbitrary, capricious, unsupported by the facts and "the product of political pressure".

The US military's headquarters at the Pentagon expanded its blacklist of alleged "Chinese military companies" on June 8 to 188 entities.

"This decision relieves the company from further adverse consequences of the 1260H designation," WuXi AppTec said in a filing to the Hong Kong bourse on Tuesday morning, referring to the list that is kept under section 1260H of a US defence law.

"We remain committed to serving our customers and enabling the lifesaving and life-improving medicines they make for patients," the company added. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK, regional markets get a bump from Wall St gains
articles.excerpt: Asian stocks rose on Tuesday as a drop in oil prices after US President Donald Trump said he planned to…
articles.fullText:
Asian stocks rose on Tuesday as a drop in oil prices after US President Donald Trump said he planned to hold off on new military strikes against Iran lifted sentiment ahead of US inflation data that could sway the near-term interest rate outlook.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index opened up 172 points, or 0.7 percent, at 24,621.

The China enterprises index rose 38 points, or 0.47 percent, to 8,298 while the tech index climbed 31 points, or 0.78 percent, to 4,072.

Two chip-sector firms debuted in Hong Kong, with AI chip designer Suzhou Denglin Technology falling into loss territory at the start of trading and semiconductor packager and tester Jiangsu Xinde Semiconductor Technology making a much stronger debut.

Across the border, the Shanghai Composite Index opened up 21 points, or 0.58 percent, at 3,682.

The Shenzhen Component Index put on 167 points, or 1.51 percent, to open at 11,313 while the ChiNext Index rose 59 points, or 2.44 percent, to 2,518.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei opened 596 points, or 1.02 percent, higher at 59,372 and was 1,725 points or almost three percent higher at one stage before noon.

In Seoul, the Kospi surged 228 points, or 4.55 percent, to open at 5,247 amid gains for its heavyweight chipmakers – 3.74 percent for Samsung Electronics and 5.28 percent for SK Hynix.

The gains came as Brent crude futures were hovering at their lowest levels since early September, well below US$100 per barrel, as investors pinned their hopes on possible talks between the United States and Iran.

They were last down one percent at US$91.56 a barrel.

The US-Israeli war with Iran, which erupted at the end of February, has stoked inflationary concerns across the globe, spurring major central banks to raise rates in recent months.

Nick Twidale, chief market strategist at ATFX Global, said the latest developments offered hope that an end to the conflict could be approaching, but there was still a considerable gap between diplomacy and a lasting peace agreement.

"The risk now is that markets have moved too far, too quickly... any indication that negotiations are faltering could see a substantial rebound in prices as traders rapidly rebuild the geopolitical risk premium," he said.

The slump in oil prices eased inflation worries and helped lift stocks after last week's rout as a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections fed concerns that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade.

On Monday, the S&P 500 clocked its biggest one-day jump since April, closing up 2.35 percent while the Nasdaq closed 2.7 percent higher, its best day in over four months.

"We believe resets in expectations are healthy, and the AI trade appears to be working through a reset of its own at the moment," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise.

Earnings reports due this week from tech companies such as CoreWeave, a barometer of investor anxiety over AI, will be another test for markets as investors fret about the cost of the AI buildout.

Saglimbene said Anthropic's prospective IPO could be an important test of investor confidence.

Market focus remains on Nvidia after the second-most valuable company in the world said its board was probing whether CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation.

A media report alleged he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.

Huang has said he was unfaithful to his wife.

Shares of Nvidia, which is due to report earnings next week, fell 4.2 percent.

Daniel Morgan, a portfolio manager at Synovus Trust who holds Nvidia shares, said certain personalities in the technology space were so intertwined with the success of the company it was hard to separate the two.

"But the companies can still be successful long after the original founders have taken on a lesser role," he said, adding he remained confident that Nvidia would continue to maintain its lead in the GPU AI chip market even if Huang was forced to step down to a lesser role.

All eyes will be on US inflation data later in the day, with prices likely to have increased at a moderate pace in October, economists said, and remaining stubbornly high enough for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates next month.

Traders are pricing in an 84 percent chance of a rate hike next month versus 74 percent a week earlier, a CME FedWatch tool showed after a blowout October jobs report on Friday. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: A trip to the South Korean seaside for glimpses of my North Korean hometown
articles.excerpt: Escapee Park Sol-ji often gets homesick for the port city of Chongjin. A beach day in Busan comes close.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
Park Sol-ji stared out over the water at Gwangalli Beach with the iconic Gwangan Bridge in the distance, just above the horizon. South Korea’s touristy second largest city of Busan is a drastic change from heavily industrialized Chongjin – her hometown in North Korea. But both cities are large ports on the eastern side of the peninsula, and the sand, the breeze, and the smell of the sea reminds her of home.
“I love looking at the sea, and coming here whenever I miss my hometown is a big part of it,” she told Radio Free Asia Nov. 3. “Also, coming to the seaside makes me feel like I can finally breathe. I think I like it because it gives me such a sense of liberation.”
Park Sol-ji is a pseudonym she is using for safety reasons. Sol-ji fled North Korea 19 years ago when she was 20 years old, arriving in South Korea the following year. Adjusting to life in the fast-paced South was jarring. Though she tried her best to blend in among South Korean 20-somethings , it would all come crashing down whenever she spoke with her unmistakable North Korean accent.
She often found the degree of change in her life to be overwhelming, and she longed to return home, but that was now impossible. In times like that a trip to the sea would always remind her just enough of home to boost her spirits.
These days, she’s shed the accent and looks about the same as everyone else, but she still gets homesick and often travels to the seaside.
A map showing the locations of Chongjin, North Korea and Busan, South Korea.
(RFA) Busan is very different from Chongjin. Though both cities are industrialized ports, the South Korean city has – over many decades – invested in travel infrastructure and branded itself as a global tourist destination.
According to tourism statistics compiled by the Busan city government, more than 3.93 million foreign tourists have already visited Busan this year alone. CNN introduced Busan as “Asia’s Next Coastal City,” and Expedia selected Busan as the only Korean destination among its “Top 10 Destinations of the Year for 2027.”
But for Sol-ji, it’s not the glitz and glamor she’s coming for. She is here to take in the memories of the seaside of her childhood, where she played in the sand with her friends and spent precious moments with her family.
Memories roll in with the rising tide
Though the forecast called for cloudy weather, Gwangalli Beach had quite a few visitors from midday, perhaps due to the unexpectedly clear sky. Couples were taking photos with the sea as a backdrop, groups of noisy students on a field trip made their way across the sand, and foreign tourists walked barefoot. Everyone had smiles on their faces. Gwangalli Beach is well known as a romantic spot where the blue sea harmonizes with the spectacular night view of the Gwangan Bridge.
Sol-ji slowly surveyed the seascape and her face lit up as she spoke of the days she and her family would break out a large cauldron, build a fire, catch fish, and cook eojuk, a type of spicy fish porridge. She also remembered how she and her friends used to play by pulling up seaweed to gather in makeshift nets made of their extra clothes. Although these were ordinary childhood games, looking back now, they were moments she can never have again. To her, the sea is a landscape she longs for, as well as a place where she finds solace for her wounds.
“I even dreamt of returning to Chongjin because I missed my hometown, but even in the dream, seeing my dyed hair and decorated nails, I thought I would get caught,” she said. North Korea is notorious for fashion police who crack down on “capitalist” looks like dyed hair, colored nails, blue jeans, clothing with English words and phrases, and other no-nos. In South Korea, Sol-ji is free to dress how she wants to, but that does not erase her longing.
“I really do want to go back just once.”
The old village in the hills
Prior to visiting the beach, Sol-ji had started the day with a train ride to Busan Station, disembarking in the morning. The first spot on her itinerary was Gamcheon Culture Village, a 10-minute taxi ride away. The village started as a ramshackle town built up in the hills for laborers, and it expanded greatly with the swell of refugees fleeing to Busan from the advancing North Korean army in the opening weeks of the 1950-53 Korean War. In recent years the village was painstakingly restored through cultural preservation and beautification projects.
These days, tourists flock to its narrow meandering streets, attracted by the colorfully painted houses, many of which have been converted to shops, cafes and mini-museums. Near the high point of the village sits a colorful statue of the Little Prince, presiding over a space dedicated to the mythos presented in Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s world-renowned novella.
A statue of the Little Prince and the fox at the Little Prince House in Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, South Korea.
(Saha-gu Office via korea.net) Today, the tourists have come in force. More often than not, passersby who came for the village’s unique artsy flair will be speaking in a language other than Korean.
While most tourists are browsing the shops, ordering refreshments, or taking in one of the museums, Sol-ji slowly looks around the alley, finally focusing on a clothesline in the courtyard of one house. She noticed three or four items of clothing hanging on a single line, swaying in the breeze. It was this evidence that people actually live here that conjured up the feelings of her childhood.
“People here hang their laundry on clotheslines like that. It’s exactly the same in North Korea,” she said. She explained that in North Korea some families have washing machines, but rolling blackouts are common in most places, so people still have to do laundry by hand.
“So here they also dry their laundry in the sun,” she said. “Knowing this is quite heartwarming.”
In another area of town she operated a manual pump that once drew water out of the ground. She said it made her think of her grandmother’s house in Chongjin.
Sol-ji walked along, looking around every corner of the alley. Though sun-dried laundry and the hand pump might be similar details, the nature of this town, built up on a hillside, would never make sense in Chongjin, she said.
Park Sol-ji, visits Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “There aren’t many houses on slopes like this in Chongjin. It costs a lot of money to build roads and houses up to these inclines,” she said. “Instead, there are many fields on these mountain slopes. It is land where people make a living through farming.”
Noon approached, and it was time for lunch.
Food for reminiscing
Sol-ji’s next destination was the famous open-air Jagalchi seafood market. As she walked from stall to stall, the boisterous calls of merchants mingled together, as they tried to attract customers by shouting out prices in their folksy Busan accents while holding up wriggling fish. Jagalchi is the largest seafood market in the country, and it is another big Busan tourist destination.
Sol-ji looked around the market, carefully observing the fish leaping out of the ice. She seemed to be searching for familiar fish such as flounder, cutlassfish, mackerel, and squid. Although it was an unfamiliar market, the seafood displayed on the stalls was something she often saw back in her hometown, she said.
She recalled how North and South Koreans use different words for squid and two types of octopus and this led to confusion.
문어 (muneo) 낙지 (nakji) 오징어 (ojingeo)
North Korea all octopus varieties squid cuttlefish
South Korea large octopus varieties small octopus varieties squid and cuttlefish
“We called squid nakji . So when I’m here and I see the small octopus that they’re calling nakji , that’s what we used to call baby muneo ,” said Sol-ji.
She recalled that during her childhood she would often snack on dried squid, tearing off tasty parts and chewing it by the mouthful.
The marketplace also conjured up memories of eating raw fish, but the way she enjoyed it up North was very different. In Chongjin raw fish is served slathered in a thick sauce, and wrapped with other ingredients in lettuce. But she was surprised when she came to South Korea and saw people eat the plain white flesh dipped in only a little bit of sauce.
Park Sol-ji visits Jagalchi seafood market in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “I think the seafood I ate in Chongjin was tastier,” she said, smiling broadly. She explained that fish caught in colder places is saltier and tastier.
But then again, she said, it might have just been that she was hungry all the time back then.
“It’s like something out of a dream.”
As the sun set behind Gwangalli Beach, Gwangan Bridge lit up the night sky in a dazzling flash of color. Sol-ji got in line to ride a yacht under the bridge, out to sea to catch the fireworks show exclusively for the passengers.
Park Sol-ji views the city of Busan, South Korea at night off Gwangalli Beach, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) As the yacht moved along, Sol-ji couldn’t help but notice that it was a stark difference from the pitch black nighttime seascape in Chongjin – out at sea, Busan’s night sky is brightly and colorfully illuminated by the bridge, the cityscape – and soon, the fireworks.
Sol-ji sat on the deck, quietly closing her eyes and feeling the sea breeze. Then in one magic moment, lights shot out of the sky with a loud boom. The fireworks brought a bright smile across her face.
In all her excitement, her thoughts drifted to her childhood friends. Although they live in different places now, she thought how wonderful it would be if they could gaze at the dazzling night sea of ​​Busan together.
A yacht tour fireworks display in the waters off Gwangalli Beach in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “This really feels like a dream, but I really do want to try it with them at least once,” she said. “I want to take lots of photos with my friends and go sightseeing like this.”
Under the glowing bursts, she reflected on her current daily life. Nothing like this would ever be possible in North Korea, she said. But in South Korea she can go wherever she wants, with whomever she wants, wearing whatever she wants. She smiled, realizing that “freedom” isn’t a grandiose ideal or political buzzword, it is contained in an ordinary moment like this, on a boat at sea near Busan, under the brightly lit night sky.
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: Harris Ho wins HK's second gold at Youth Olympics
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong, China fencer Harris Ho on Tuesday bagged the city's second gold medal of the Youth Olympics Games in…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong, China fencer Harris Ho on Tuesday bagged the city's second gold medal of the Youth Olympics Games in Senegal, winning the individual men's foil final in dominant fashion.

Ho, the reigning world junior foil champion, defeated Japan's Masashi Maeda 15-8 in the gold medal bout at the Dakar Expo Centre.

The 17-year-old's triumph marks the SAR's first-ever individual fencing gold in the history of the Youth Olympics, with the city having previously claimed two fencing silvers in the 2014 and 2018 editions of the quadrennial event.

Ho's win caps off a dominant run in the competition, going five and one in the group stage to enter the quarter-finals as the second seed.

The SAR star brushed aside the Czech Republic's Krystof Novak 15-2 in the quarter-finals, before beating Cyprus's Aris Kiayias 15-10 in the last four.

The landmark victory also builds on a phenomenal year for Ho, who won the Cadet World Championship title in April, and further cements him as a top contender ahead of the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law congratulated him on capturing gold in Senegal.

"With an outstanding performance at the Youth Olympic Games this year, he overcame his opponents to secure the gold medal and set a historic milestone for a young Hong Kong fencing athlete. All of the Hong Kong citizens take great pride in his remarkable achievement," she said in a statement.

articles.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
articles.excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox…
articles.fullText:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first,  sign up here .

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.

Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).

The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. 

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.

But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

articles.title: China slams 'baseless' claims it spied on Nvidia boss
articles.excerpt: Beijing rejected on Monday claims that it had spied on Jensen Huang, chief executive of US chip giant Nvidia, calling…
articles.fullText:
Beijing rejected on Monday claims that it had spied on Jensen Huang, chief executive of US chip giant Nvidia, calling the allegations "baseless".

"We have responded to this matter previously. The narrative of a so-called Chinese spy is entirely baseless vilification and smearing," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing.

He was speaking after Nvidia's board announced it had opened a probe into media reports alleging "a foreign intelligence effort" and Huang's acknowledgement that he had an affair with a woman.

Late last month, The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials concluded that Alice Huang, a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed, had been funnelling information to Beijing.

The executive, also known as Huang Le, developed a close relationship with the 63-year-old Nvidia boss, the Times said.

In a message to company employees released on Sunday, the Nvidia chief acknowledged having an affair and apologised to his family and company staff.

"I was unfaithful to my wife," he said.

"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

Jensen Huang is a huge figure in the artificial intelligence revolution and a close informal adviser to US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly spoken out against regulating the industry so as not to let China gain the upper hand in the AI race.

The issue of AI is likely to arise during Trump's planned talks with President Xi Jinping this month at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen.

Asked whether the Nvidia chief would be joining his trip to Asia, which includes the Apec summit in Shenzhen next week, Trump said: "I don't know but I'll certainly take him."

Trump said Huang was "a fine person, but you never know what's going on. I'm sure – I hope everything's fine. He's done such an incredible job." (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Trump says Shenzhen talks with Xi and Putin likely
articles.excerpt: US President Donald Trump on Sunday said he expects to meet with President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin…
articles.fullText:
US President Donald Trump on Sunday said he expects to meet with President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen scheduled for November 18-19.

"Well, I'm going to be going to China," he said, "and one of the meetings I think will be with President Putin and President Xi, and that'll be interesting."

He added: "We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearisation, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran."

The Kremlin said on October 21 that this first of its kind trilateral meeting is "being prepared".

This followed a Wall Street Journal report that Putin wanted the three-way talks to broker a peace deal to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Death toll mounts to 14 in Shanxi fire
articles.excerpt: The death toll from a fire at a building in Taiyuan, capital of northern Shanxi province, has risen to 14…
articles.fullText:
The death toll from a fire at a building in Taiyuan, capital of northern Shanxi province, has risen to 14, local authorities said on Monday.

The fire broke out at the building in the city's Yingze District at 4.59pm on Sunday, with the fire department saying the building is on Liuxiang South Road.

The death toll update followed an earlier report that 38 people had been sent to hospitals, with five of them being declared dead. (Xinhua)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Chinese inflation spikes at plants and cools in shops
articles.excerpt: China's producer inflation accelerated to its fastest pace in nearly four-and-a-half years while consumer inflation cooled in October, data showed…
articles.fullText:
China's producer inflation accelerated to its fastest pace in nearly four-and-a-half years while consumer inflation cooled in October, data showed on Monday, reflecting persistent cost pressures from higher oil prices despite weak domestic demand.

Global oil prices remained elevated during much of last month, raising costs for coal mining, oil and natural gas extraction processing, chemicals and other energy-intensive sectors, a key driver of producer-price inflation.

Those upstream price pressures have yet to fully feed through to consumers amid soft demand conditions.

The producer price index climbed by 5.7 percent from a year earlier, compared with a five percent increase in September, beating economists' forecasts for a 5.3 percent gain in a poll, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed.

The consumer price index rose by 0.7 percent year on year, after a 0.9 percent rise in September, to come in just below economists' expectations for a 0.8 percent increase.

On a monthly basis, the CPI matched forecasts for an unchanged outcome after edging up 0.2 percent in September.

While the world's second-largest economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, buoyed by resilient exports, weak household demand has continued to constrain consumer spending.

Ongoing trade tensions and an increasingly uncertain global outlook are also clouding the outlook for exports.

External shocks are having a greater impact, while the imbalance between robust supply and weak domestic demand remains pronounced, said an official at China's state planner last month.

China's struggling stock market, where AI-related stocks have tumbled from lofty valuations on concerns about AI demand and export restrictions targeting China, could further weigh on consumer spending.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, eased to 0.8 percent in October from one percent in September, offering a gauge of underlying price pressures in the economy. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Lopez double fires Barcelona to top of La Liga
articles.excerpt: Fermin Lopez struck twice to help Barcelona come from behind to beat Atletico Madrid 2-1 and move three points clear…
articles.fullText:
Fermin Lopez struck twice to help Barcelona come from behind to beat Atletico Madrid 2-1 and move three points clear at the top of La Liga.

The Spanish champions lead second place Real Madrid, who beat Valencia 3-0 on Saturday, with Atletico third, now five points behind.

Giuliano Simeone fired Atletico ahead in a high-octane start, before Lopez pulled Barca level shortly before the interval at the Metropolitano stadium.

The 23-year-old Spain international netted the winner after 66 minutes when Lamine Yamal slipped him in, helped Barca triumph despute not being at their best.

Last season Atletico defeated Barcelona in the Champions League quarter-finals and also in the Copa del Rey, but the Catalans earned some measure of revenge here.

"Coming off last season, when they beat us... we knew what they were going to offer – a very difficult game," Lopez told Movistar.

"It got tricky for us in the first half with their goal, but I think we knew how to come back and we had a great match."

Atletico captain Koke said his team would not let the defeat, their first in La Liga since September 5, upset them.

"I think the team had a really great first half. We had chances to kill off the game and we didn't take, them," said Koke.

"That's football – it's about being clinical, and they were more clinical than we were.

"But there's nothing to criticise the team for, we have to keep going like this because there's still a long way to go in La Liga."

Earlier on, fourth-place Real Betis earned a 2-0 win at Elche, while Real Sociedad, fifth, defeated Rayo Vallecano 1-0.

Villarreal beat Getafe 2-0 to move eighth and Celta Vigo and Levante shared a goalless draw. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Norris wins Brazil; Mercedes take constructors' title
articles.excerpt: Lando Norris picked his way through the rainstorms on Sunday to claim a second consecutive victory for McLaren in the…
articles.fullText:
Lando Norris picked his way through the rainstorms on Sunday to claim a second consecutive victory for McLaren in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix as Mercedes clinched the constructors' championship and a famous title double.

The 26-year-old outgoing 2025 world champion came home 14.6 seconds clear of Red Bull's four-time champion Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar to record his 14th career victory and the 50th podium.

Verstappen started from 21st on the grid and delivered another bravura drive while George Russell finished fourth, after starting fifth and spinning in the pitlane, for Mercedes ahead of teammate Kimi Antonelli, who finished fifth, seven days after becoming the youngest champion.

The 20-year-old had started from the front row alongside pole-sitter Norris and endured a difficult race, but it was enough to ensure that Mercedes outscored Ferrari to take a ninth teams' title.

"That was a very tough race," said Norris.

"It was difficult with the launches off the line, a lot of challenges, going to slicks in the wet and so tough when you are pushing! But I kept it cool and made no mistakes and it is nice to be on the top step again."

Verstappen said: "It was a challenging race! The first laps were so important. We were strong on the inters, but then it was not so good but starting P21 and finishing on the podium is a good result."

Hadjar, having taken his third podium of the year and led a Grand Prix for the first time, added: "That was so difficult. The switching from inters to softs and then back again! Very tricky to drive and then more rain."

The race began with a spectacular opening lap as Antonelli, with an excellent start, led into the Senna Esses as Norris struggled from his 20th pole and Lawson moved up to third in the Curva do Sol.

Behind them, Lewis Hamilton and Verstappen made light of their back-of-the-grid starts and were ninth and 10th within two laps as plumes of spray rose throughout the field.

By lap six, Norris had recovered to pass Liam Lawson while Antonelli was 5.1 seconds clear and instructed to keep his tyres cool. All were on intermediates as the track began to dry with heavy rain forecast.

Verstappen and Antonelli delayed their stops, allowing Norris to take advantage of his earlier stop to warm his tyres and, when Antonelli spun at the start of lap 20 on cold rubber, he took the lead.

On lap 50, Norris pitted again, returning third behind McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri, who let him by, before he took second when Hadjar pitted on lap 51, leaving the 2025 champion 7.4 seconds behind his successor.

Antonelli came in again on lap 55, handing Norris the lead. Again. He rejoined fifth behind Russell, with the Red Bulls second and third. It began drizzling and then intensified into rain.

Norris pitted on lap 63 for intermediate tyres, followed by Verstappen and the rest, with Antonelli released into the exit path of Franco Colapinto and Hamilton spinning - as conditions worsened in the final laps. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Alcaraz downs Shelton to win Paris Masters
articles.excerpt: Carlos Alcaraz gained a measure of revenge on Ben Shelton on Sunday as the seven-time Grand Slam champion beat the…
articles.fullText:
Carlos Alcaraz gained a measure of revenge on Ben Shelton on Sunday as the seven-time Grand Slam champion beat the American 7-6 (7/5), 7-5 to win the Paris Masters for the first time.

In defeating the man who ended his US Open title defence earlier this season, the 23-year-old claimed the ninth 1000-level title of his career.

Unlike their five-set quarter-final epic in New York two months ago, the clash in Paris lasted just under two hours.

"For me it's really special that finally I just got to play great tennis," Alcaraz told reporters. "I went far in the tournament, lifting the trophy at the end.

"I would say this week I took a step forward mentally. I had a lot of really tough moments.

"I'm just really happy that I controlled my emotions, controlled my thoughts every moment, every single match," he added in reference to his quarter-final win against Taylor Fritz in which he saved two match points.

Coming into Paris on the back of winning the 500-level title in Vienna, Alcaraz has won his last nine matches.

"Probably these two last weeks have been the best I've played since my comeback," Alcaraz added of his return from a wrist injury that caused him to miss the French Open and Wimbledon.

Ahead of the ATP Finals, which run November 15-22 in Turin, world number three Alcaraz now holds five tour-level titles this year – only the injured Jannik Sinner has more with six.

In Italy, he will next be seeking a first coronation at the season-ending Finals.

For world number four Shelton, it was a first defeat in a Masters final after winning his two previous appearances in showpiece matches at that level – both coming in the last two editions of the Canadian Open.

An entertaining first set which drew a multitude of admiring gasps from the crowd went the distance despite both players enjoying some success on the other's serve.

In the tie-break, a Shelton error at 4-4 followed by a leaping backhand smash by Alcaraz brought up two set points.

The first came and went when Alcaraz thundered the ball into the top of the net cord and the expectant arena froze in time as it rose and fell in seeming slow motion, only to land on the Spaniard's side of the court.

Alcaraz was not to be denied a second time, however, as Shelton overcooked a forehand on the next point to cede the opener.

At 2-2 in the second set, Shelton let out a bellow of frustration after missing a groundstroke at 15-30 on Alcaraz's serve, but the American could smile at the end of the game as a double fault and missed forehand produced the first break of the match.

Alcaraz had said after booking his spot in the final that his reflexes would need to be "ten out of ten" when facing Shelton's serve and they were just that three games later as he levelled the set at four-all.

A deft exchange of angled drop shots ended by an Alcaraz winner down the line brought the Spaniard's finger to his ear and the crowd again to their feet as Shelton suddenly found himself serving to keep the final alive.

He did so at the first time of asking but when required to serve again to force a breaker, Shelton cracked as Alcaraz again pounced to seal the title with a flicked backhand winner.

"It's all about the little details. The difference in our match in the US Open was the little details, and same here," 24-year-old Shelton said.

"I've learned so much, and it's the position that I want to be in.

"Playing in the US Open final against (Alexander) Zverev, playing the finals here against Carlos, now going to Turin and get to line up against the eight best players in the world."

After winning two French Opens and now the Paris Masters, former world number one Alcaraz is undefeated in title matches in the city, excluding the Olympic Games which do not carry ranking points.

In the earlier doubles final, French pair Quentin Halys and Pierre-Hugues Herbert upset second seeds Neal Skupski and Christian Harrison as the wildcards triumphed 7-6 (7/3), 6-7 (4/7), 10-8. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Man Utd fight back to draw with Villa; Chelsea stunned
articles.excerpt: Manchester United rescued an incredible 4-4 draw against Aston Villa as two stoppage-time goals gave Michael Carrick renewed hope of…
articles.fullText:
Manchester United rescued an incredible 4-4 draw against Aston Villa as two stoppage-time goals gave Michael Carrick renewed hope of avoiding the sack, while Chelsea suffered a shock 1-0 loss at Sunderland on Sunday.

United boss Carrick was seconds away from heading into the international break on the back of another devastating defeat that would surely have led to his dismissal.

But Carrick's side struck twice in the six minutes of additional time through Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu to leave their manager's future still uncertain.

United are in the relegation zone and have not won in their last eight Premier League matches, so it is far from sure that Carrick will survive the axe.

He had earned a stay of execution when United's hierarchy allowed him to remain in charge despite last weekend's loss at Chelsea.

United responded by ending a nine-match winless run in all competitions as they came from two goals down to beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League on Tuesday.

But United, who have only three wins in 15 games this season, were back in turmoil when they fell 2-0 down against Villa in the first four minutes at Old Trafford.

Alysson struck in the first minute with a shot that squirmed under United keeper Senne Lammens.

Nicolas Jackson slotted in the second three minutes later after a weak save from Lammens pushed the ball into his path.

Bruno Fernandes got one back with a 16th-minute penalty after Boubacar Kamara fouled Matheus Cunha before former Villa midfielder Youri Tielemans slammed in United's 44th-minute equaliser.

Villa's John McGinn converted a 48th-minute penalty following Diogo Dalot's clumsy challenge on Alysson.

Leon Goretzka poked in Villa's fourth from close-range after United's Leny Yoro headed against his own crossbar in the 53rd minute.

Yet Zirkzee's stoppage-time finish gave United hope and Dorgu headed their dramatic equaliser in the final seconds after a weak punch from Villa keeper Zion Suzuki.

Carrick wore a bewildered look on his face as he walked down the tunnel towards an uncertain future, with United next in action at Liverpool on November 22.

"Making it hard for ourselves. The goals are coming from individual mistakes. We need to tighten up," Carrick said.

"But I thought we were the better team. If we get one, then anything can happen. We never gave up and never stopped believing."

Chelsea arrived at the Stadium of Light hoping to bolster their bid to qualify for the Champions League via a top-four finish.

Instead, they departed red-faced after an embarrassing loss to third-bottom Sunderland, who celebrated a league victory for only the second time this season.

Fifth-placed Chelsea have already been beaten four times in 10 league matches under former Real Madrid boss Xabi Alonso.

Chelsea were rocked in the 36th minute when Enzo Le Fee converted a penalty after Brian Brobbey was up-ended by Levi Colwill.

"We were not creating enough chances in the final third against the low block. We were not controlling and sustaining the attack there," Alonso said.

Liverpool got back on track with a 3-1 win at lowly Crystal Palace.

The Reds had been beaten by Arsenal and Fenerbahce before arriving in south London, sparking pointed questions about Andoni Iraola in the former Bournemouth manager's first season in charge.

But Alexis Mac Allister headed Liverpool in front from Dominik Szoboszlai's cross after 40 minutes.

Florian Wirtz bagged Liverpool's second with a composed finish from Bradley Barcola's cross in the 54th minute.

Alexander Isak finished off Wirtz's pass in the 89th minute to wrap up fourth-placed Liverpool's much-needed victory after a two-game losing streak.

Eddie Nketiah's stoppage-time penalty after a foul by Milos Kerkez was no consolation for bottom of the table Palace.

Brighton extended their superb start to the season, climbing to second place with a 2-0 win against Brentford at the Amex Stadium.

Diego Gomez put Brighton ahead early on before Brentford striker Igor Thiago was sent off.

Pascal Gross doubled Brighton's advantage with a 42nd minute penalty.

The Seagulls' sixth win in their last seven league games lifted them within five points of champions Arsenal, who beat Hull on Saturday.

Bournemouth striker Evanilson maintained his hot streak with a goal in a 2-1 win at Ipswich. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: North Korean orphans fast tracked into state care to stem declining birth rate
articles.excerpt: Orphanages are now supplied more regularly after shift toward birth-friendly policies.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean
North Korea is attempting to address its decreasing birth rate by improving the conditions of state-run orphanages while increasing crackdowns on illegal abortions, residents in the country told Radio Free Asia.
The total fertility rate for North Korea is estimated to be 1.59 children per woman of childbearing age according to key statistical indicators from South Korea’s Ministry of Data and Statistics. This is well below the replacement fertility rate of 2.1 required to maintain the population.
The rate may be even lower than estimated, a 2025 report by the Washington-based Stimson Center’s 38 North project said.
Orphanages and nurseries were previously poorly supplied, meaning that taking in more children was difficult, but government policies have improved the situation, with supplies of milk, food, clothing and shoes flowing in more regularly, the residents said.
School children arrive to pay their respects before the statues of late North Korean leaders Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il at Mansu Hill in Pyongyang on Sept. 9, 2023.
(Kim Won Jin/AFP) “Recently, authorities have been more quickly sending orphaned children or children born to unmarried women to nurseries or orphanages,” a resident of the country’s northeastern province of North Hamgyong, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told RFA. “The residents’ reaction to this is generally positive.”
The resident talked about a situation where an unmarried woman from Kyongwon county, on the border with China, had to give up her child because of the difficulty raising it alone. The child was quickly accepted into an orphanage in October.
Though the resident did not specify how long it took to place the child, another resident, from nearby South Hamgyong province, told RFA that in another case, in the coastal city of Tanchon, it took about a month.
“In September, in Tanchon, a 6-year-old child became an orphan after his mother, who had been raising him alone, died of illness,” the South Hamgyong resident said on condition of anonymity to speak freely. The child “went to an orphanage after about a month.”
Supplies meeting demand
The government’s apparent priority on supplying nurseries and orphanages has come after a series of child-friendly policies were enacted including the Childcare Law of 2022 and the Law on Preferential Treatment for Multi-Child Families of 2025. Authorities actively encourage childbirth and child-rearing, including by pushing propaganda messaging that “having many babies is patriotism.”
A woman receives the "Communist Mother's Honor Award" during the Fifth National Mothers' Convention in Pyongyang, North Korea, Dec. 4, 2023.
(KCNA via KNS/AFP) The country’s leader Kim Jong Un famously was brought to tears in 2023 when he publicly discussed the declining birth rate at the National Mothers’ Conference in December 2023.
“Putting our efforts into raising the birth rate together with mothers is a critical revolutionary undertaking that cannot be resolved by the power of our Party and government alone,” he said at the event.
Sources in RFA reports after that incident explained that women were reluctant to marry and have kids because they wanted to focus on their own happiness.
Abortion crackdown
Another way the government has been trying to prevent a declining birth rate is to punish doctors who perform abortions .
By law, abortion is illegal in North Korea, but in practice, some doctors accept payment to perform the procedure in secret.
But these days, those doctors are harder to find, the North Hamgyong resident said.
“There are women who come home pregnant after serving in the military, and they try to get rid of the baby quickly before it is seen by others,” the North Hamgyong resident said. “But recently, abortion procedures have not been easy, so many end up giving birth.”
Unwanted pregnancies happen often in North Korea because sex education is non-existent, the North Hamgyong resident said. But even if the mother gives birth, administrative hurdles and societal pressure make it very difficult to raise the child. This is because it is impossible to register the child without the father, and because of the stigma surrounding unwed mothers.
Many unwed mothers are finding creative ways to put their children born out of wedlock in orphanages without having any official record of the birth, the South Hamgyong resident said. “In late September in Tanchon, a resident found a baby wrapped in a sling in a neighborhood alley and took it to the community center.”
Students attend class in North Korea, April 2, 2018.
(KCNA via Reuters) However, it was later revealed that the person who took the child to the community center was actually the maternal uncle of the woman who had given birth, the South Hamgyong resident said. Since the fact that the unmarried woman had given birth might become a major obstacle to marriage if known to the outside world, the uncle had resorted to a workaround for his niece.
The South Hamgyong resident said that the woman did not intend to become pregnant, and had tried to get an abortion but she could not find any doctor willing to provide one.
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: International community condemns Joshua Wong’s 10-year ‘foreign collusion’ sentence
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong democracy activist has been in prison since age 23 and is expected to be released around 2036 at…
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Mandarin
After a Hong Kong court sentenced pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison Thursday for foreign collusion, international lawmakers, activists, and rights organizations condemned the decision saying it violates human rights.
Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong gets 10 more years under security law
Wong, 30, is one of the most internationally recognizable faces of the now-quashed democracy movement in the city. He was among 45 Hong Kong opposition politicians and pro-democracy activists who were convicted of “conspiracy to commit subversion” under the city’s draconian 2020 National Security Law for taking part in a democratic primary in the summer of 2020. Wong in September pleaded guilty to “conspiracy to endanger national security with foreign or external forces.”
On Thursday, Judge Tam Yiu-ho of the Hong Kong High Court ruled that the case constituted a “serious offense” under the security law, which carries a starting sentence of 13 years. It was later reduced to 10 years in light of his guilty plea.
Wong had already been serving a four-year-and-eight-month sentence for the subversion charge and had been due for release in January, but under the current decision, he will not be released until 2036, when he is 40 years old.
Louis Lee, Joshua Wong's friend, shows a photograph with Joshua Wong in a book published by a pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism in Hong Kong, on Aug. 20, 2026.
(Chan Long Hei/AP) The sentence was “utterly shameless,” Chinese democracy activist Wang Dan, who was a student leader in the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and who now lives in exile in the United States, said in a statement.
“For a regime that claims to be powerful to pursue and persecute a young student in this manner only highlights its insecurity and brutality,” said Wang. “Joshua Wong campaigned and advocated for Hong Kong’s freedom. If that is considered a crime, then the real criminals are the authorities who forced a young person onto the streets in the first place.”
International condemnation
Joshua Wong’s pro-democracy activities are not criminal, Phil Robertson, Director of the Bangkok-based rights group the Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates, said in a statement.
“It’s supremely ironic that China, one of the biggest practitioners of transnational repression in the world, has now sentenced Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison for daring to seek international solidarity to resist that repression,” Robertson said. “Holding meetings with international activists and foreign government officials, talking to the global media, and mounting petition drives are the day to day work of human rights activists, and shouldn’t be criminalized.”
Wong is a hero and the charges against him have no standing, U.S. representative John Moolenaar, Chair of the House Select Committee on China, said in a statement.
“Joshua only pleaded guilty to the baseless charge of foreign collusion because of the CCP’s systematic erosion of Hong Kong’s judicial independence,” he said, using the abbreviation for the Chinese Communist Party. “In return, the CCP has effectively sentenced him under its repressive National Security Law.”
Moolenaar said the sentencing showed China’s “complete disregard” for universal rights.
Hong Kong protest leader Joshua Wong, 22, speaks as thousands of protesters surrounding the police headquarters in Hong Kong on June 21, 2019.
(Paula Bronstein/Getty Images) “Joshua and Hong Kong need the international community’s support now more than ever,” he said. “He should be immediately released and reunited with his family.”
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council, or MAC, issued a statement after the sentencing, strongly condemning Hong Kong authorities for continuing to infringe upon the basic human rights under the guise of national security.
The MAC statement said the Hong Kong government’s renewed heavy sentencing under the National Security Law is a continued political prosecution of pro-democracy figures, including Wong, who has been detained for more than 2,000 days since 2020.
The statement called on Beijing and Hong Kong authorities to stop using national security as a pretext to suppress pro-democracy activists and to immediately release those detained for exercising their basic rights.
“Domestic support” for “overseas operations”
The charges allege that between July 1 and November 23, 2020, Wong conspired with Nathan Law, another prominent pro-democracy figure who was in exile overseas, and others to request foreign governments or organizations to impose sanctions, blockades, or other actions deemed hostile by the authorities on China and Hong Kong.
The judge held that after the Hong Kong National Security Law came into effect, Nathan Law continued to push for sanctions overseas, while Wong shared related content through foreign media and social media platforms, attracting the attention of foreign governments and providing support from Hong Kong for overseas initiatives. The judge rejected the defense’s claim that Wong’s role was limited, believing that Wong and Law collaborated and that their roles were equally important.
The defense previously argued that the severity of this case was far less than other national security cases; Wong was only 23 years old when he committed the crime and has been deprived of his freedom for nearly six years, while the prosecution only brought charges after many years. The defense suggested a sentence of about four and a half years and hoped that the court would allow Wong the opportunity to take care of his parents in the future, but this was not accepted by the court.
Steve Li Kwai-Wah, chief superintendent at Hong Kong Police Force's national security department, speaks to the media at the High Court in Hong Kong, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026.
(Chan Long Hei/AP) The sentence reflected the seriousness of the case, Hong Kong Police National Security Department Chief Superintendent Steve Li Kwai-Wah said to reporters outside the court. He called on Nathan Law to return to Hong Kong and surrender.
Hong Kong and Beijing have consistently stated that their law enforcement actions are based on evidence and law, and are unrelated to the defendant’s political stance, asserting that the Hong Kong National Security Law is necessary to restore stability in Hong Kong.
Undermining freedom
Wang said that Wong’s harsh sentencing reveals that China cares little about human rights.
Student activist Joshua Wong talks on the phone after walking out of the Wanchai police station in Hong Kong on Jan. 16, 2015. A Hong Kong court sentenced Joshua Wong to 10 years in jail on November 5, 2026, for foreign collusion, extending the activist's prison term beyond the six years he has already served.
(Philippe Lopez/AFP) “This decision once again tears away the CCP’s mask, proving that it is a regime determined to be an enemy of universal values and the ideals of freedom,” he said. “Ten years – a person’s youth – spent entirely behind bars; Joshua Wong has paid such a high price. He is a hero of our times and the pride of Hong Kong. I hope everyone remembers him, follows his situation, speaks out on his behalf, and prays for him.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Overseas university heads eye NM
articles.excerpt: The World Class University Presidents Forum was held at the Hong Kong University of Science & Technology on November 4…
articles.fullText:
The World Class University Presidents Forum was held at the Hong Kong University of Science & Technology on November 4 and 5, drawing presidents and senior management from around 50 world-leading institutions.

The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government is dedicated to transforming the city into an international education hub, a vision that includes developing three university towns within the Northern Metropolis (NM).

This initiative has garnered significant attention from participating universities, with university presidents from the UK, Spain and South Africa expressing interest in exploring various models of participation.

Stuart Croft, University of Warwick Vice Chancellor & President, said the Hong Kong SAR Government is being very strategic, future-oriented and globally oriented.

"With the whole concept of economic growth being driven with universities, with industry, facilitated by government, the triple helix model, where else in the world is there something of this scale and ambition?"

Professor Croft predicted that over the next decade, the world's top universities will transform their partnership model to embedding activities.

"That is what is going to make the difference, and of course the Northern Metropolis gives a fantastic opportunity for Hong Kong universities to build that embedding process, possibly earlier, possibly more deeply than elsewhere in the world, " he said.

In the latest QS Asia University Rankings, Hong Kong has five universities in Asia’s top ten.

Mosa Moshabela, Vice Chancellor & Principal of the University of Cape Town in South Africa noted that Hong Kong’s high concentration of top-tier universities, paired with its convenient transport and lifestyle, promotes student and faculty mobility while bolstering the "Study in Hong Kong" initiative.

"I think it can really offer a good place for brain circulation. For my university, for example, it would be of interest for students and faculty to come in, especially for a relatively short stay of six months. A relatively short stay would be really good for exposure, in-depth exposure to what's happening in Hong Kong, especially if it is linked to industry."

Participating presidents also highlighted the flow of talent, which they said tends to gravitate toward places with strong innovation and research ecosystems.

They expressed hope that the Hong Kong SAR Government would proactively offer incentives to attract and retain talent and support the development of the university town project.

articles.title: HK global education role grows
articles.excerpt: Secretary for Education Choi Yuk-lin spoke today at the World Class University Presidents Forum 2026, highlighting Hong Kong's growing strength…
articles.fullText:
Secretary for Education Choi Yuk-lin spoke today at the World Class University Presidents Forum 2026, highlighting Hong Kong's growing strength, global voice and strategic vision as a premier international higher education hub. The two-day forum in Hong Kong concludes today.

Addressing the audience, Ms Choi noted that the forum gathered leaders and university presidents representing more than one-third of the world's top 50 universities. "Assembling such a distinguished constellation of global academic leadership strongly reaffirms Hong Kong's standing as an international education hub and significantly enhances the city's discourse power in the global educational arena," she said.

Ms Choi emphasised that Hong Kong's institutional strength is firmly rooted in academic excellence, robust national support and open connectivity. Citing the latest QS World University Rankings: Asia 2027, she pointed out that Hong Kong continues to set regional benchmarks with five local universities securing places among Asia's top 10.

Serving as a vital bridge between East and West, Hong Kong offers a fertile ecosystem characterised by internationalisation and diversification to bring global talent together, she said. The education chief added that the forum forms part of a strategic series of signature initiatives promoting the “Study in Hong Kong” brand worldwide, alongside major events like February’s Asia-Pacific Association for International Education Conference and Exhibition.

Elaborating on the forum's theme, "Higher Education Reimagined: Innovating for the Future", Ms Choi stressed that no matter how the global landscape evolves, universities remain fundamentally tied to economic development, societal well-being and human progress. She noted that world-leading institutions must stand at the forefront to guide this transformation as Hong Kong's educational landscape evolves.

The vision is being physically realised through the development of the Northern Metropolis University Town. The Education Bureau pointed out that under the "One Town, Five Elements" framework, the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government is building a holistic campus ecosystem integrating higher education, advanced research, market innovation, vibrant living spaces and top-tier talent.

Positioned at the gateway to the Chinese Mainland, the University Town will foster deep industry-academia-research integration, linking academic research directly with industry capabilities to serve national development under the 15th Five-Year Plan.

articles.title: Student assessment report released
articles.excerpt: The Hong Kong Examinations & Assessment Authority (HKEAA) has submitted the 2026 Territory-wide System Assessment (TSA) report to the Education…
articles.fullText:
The Hong Kong Examinations & Assessment Authority (HKEAA) has submitted the 2026 Territory-wide System Assessment (TSA) report to the Education Bureau, the Government announced today.

The report said that the performance of Primary 3 and Secondary 3 students in the three major subjects ­– Chinese Language, English Language and Mathematics – remained generally steady this year, aligning closely with results from previous assessments.

The Education Bureau welcomed the findings, noting that schools broadly agree that the TSA report provides practical data and analysis regarding student performance. Combined with internal assessment results, this information enables schools to tailor their curriculum plans and instructional strategies to enhance learning effectiveness, fully reflecting the "Assessment for Learning" ethos.

Expressing its gratitude to the school sector, the bureau commended educators for continuously adopting diversified teaching strategies to cater to the varied needs of students and raise instructional effectiveness.

The HKEAA will soon distribute school-level data directly to primary and secondary schools for feedback on learning and teaching. Meanwhile, the bureau will host thematic seminars on "Promoting Assessment for Learning" next month to support schools in making effective use of assessment data to enhance outcomes.

articles.title: Myanmar opposition forces hopeful that U.S. strategy could bring about peace
articles.excerpt: Washington’s framework includes peacemaking to increase regional influence and provide access to rare earths.
articles.fullText:
Updated at 11:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 4, 2026.
Read a version of this story in Burmese
Armed ethnic groups and members of Myanmar’s shadow government are hoping that a recently made public U.S. strategy for their country decrease fighting and bring about peace with the military-backed government, the organizations told Radio Free Asia.
The U.S. State Department recently released an Integrated Country Strategy document for Myanmar that outlines Washington’s aims to use diplomacy to promote peace in the volatile Southeast Asian country, potentially providing access to rare earth deposits dominated by China.
The policy document lays out four mission goals, which include protecting U.S. citizens, addressing trade deficits, promoting peace, and increasing U.S. regional influence through engagement.
Lwe River network, Mekong Tributary, with clusters of rare earth mines in Shan State, Myanmar, Nov. 11, 2025.
(Planet Labs via Reuters) To achieve these goals, dealing with Myanmar’s military-backed government – headed by the same people who ousted the previous government in a coup in 2021 – cannot be avoided. Washington initially shunned engagement with the military after the coup and imposed sanctions on its most senior leaders, but has since softened its stance, rolling back some sanctions and even holding high level talks in September 2026.
A U.S. State Department spokesperson on Tuesday explained the shift to RFA.
“The Administration has been evaluating how to calibrate Washington’s policy towards Burma to achieve regional stability, and also make progress on key U.S. priorities and has determined that wholesale disengagement with the authorities in Naypyidaw countered U.S. strategic interests in Burma and the region.
