We are pursuing a policy that welcomes dialogue with all stakeholders involved in the conflict as we encourage Burma to make progress on key U.S. priorities, including addressing scam centers, improving the domestic operating environment for U.S. businesses, and building towards a genuine peace process that stabilizes the country.”
Riot police man a barrier in front of the Yangon City Hall on Feb. 6, 2021, in Yangon, Myanmar.
(Getty Images) David Gum Awng, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs for the National Unity Government, or NUG, a shadow government made up of former government officials who were ousted in the 2021 coup, told RFA he understood the realities of the situation.
“The NUG respects and acknowledges that the U.S. government is actively engaging in Myanmar affairs and formulating a strategy aimed at peace, economy, and regional stability. The NUG will continue to engage in discussions with the U.S. government, Congress, and the international community including relevant partner nations.
We will also continue to urge that the U.S. government’s policies and practical actions towards Myanmar support the democratic and federal aspirations of the Myanmar people, address the root causes of the conflict, and lead toward an inclusive political resolution. International engagement in Myanmar affairs should not prolong the military dictatorship, but should aim to bring about genuine political change based on the will and rights of the people after escaping from this bad system.”
Kyaw Ni, Deputy Minister of Home Affairs and Immigration for the NUG, shared his opinion that amidst the policies of superpower nations, one must strive to achieve benefits for one’s own country.
“In this policy shift of a superpower nation, small countries suffer a lot, so a country undergoing revolution like Burma suffers even more. It is likely to be affected. Since these are superpower nations, they write policies based on their own interests. So our public also has to struggle among these policies to reach our desired revolutionary goal without harming the interests of our country, our people, and our revolution.”
The Chin National Front (CNF) soldiers in an undated photo.
(Chin Information Center) Salai Htet Ni, spokesperson for the Chin National Front, an armed ethnic rebel group, said the U.S. government needs to understand the underlying problems in Myanmar politics and get deeply involved.
“The U.S. government needs to understand the military junta’s unjust violence and killing of the people. They need to consider that. On our part, if they can perform first-stage actions like humanitarian aid for war refugees and addressing violent attacks and killings, we would welcome the U.S. involvement even more.”
Another ethnic armed group, — the Karen National Union — said U.S. involvement might reduce the amount of internal fighting, spokesperson Saw Kler Say told RFA on Wednesday.
“The new U.S. strategy could bring about changes or have a specific impact on our country from a military perspective. Firstly, it might lead to a situation where the military junta is compelled to stop its attacks targeting the civilian population.
Secondly, the U.S. might take steps — or offer recommendations — aimed at halting the ongoing internal conflicts. Politically, we also believe they are likely envisioning a political landscape that is acceptable to all parties—one that would include both the detained opposition leaders and the revolutionary forces.
To achieve sustainable peace in Myanmar by 2030, the first step must be to cease attacks targeting the civilian population. The next step involves reaching a consensus on a dialogue process aimed at ending internal conflicts; only through such a mutually agreed-upon framework can a ceasefire be attained.
In addition to these measures, all detained opposition leaders and political prisoners must be released. Without these actions, I believe that any dialogue will be extremely difficult. If detained political prisoners are excluded, meaning the process fails to be truly all inclusive, then a successful outcome may well be entirely impossible.
Regarding the emergence of a federal democracy in Myanmar, the new U.S. strategy presents both positive opportunities and concerning risks. On one hand, it could potentially lead to a genuine transition toward a federal democracy—for instance, by facilitating the abolition of the 2008 Constitution and the drafting and adoption of a new federal constitution. On the other hand, there is a risk that if the discourse is driven solely by U.S. interests, the path toward the federal democracy we envision could be diverted, creating significant challenges."
Representatives of the Kachin Independence Army and the Arakan Army responded that they were not ready to comment.
Arakan Army soldiers in an undated photo.
(Arakan Army) The Arakan Army’s Khaing Thukha asked that questions be channeled through official emails.
Hla Thein, spokesperson for the Union Solidarity and Development Party – formed by former military officers – told RFA that the U.S. strategy document is constructive for mutual interest and should be welcomed.
“Big nations becoming interested in our country, interested from a positive and beneficial perspective, should be welcomed no matter what. We have no permanent friends and no permanent enemies. If they come to cooperate fairly for our country’s interest, our people’s interest, and national interest, we will warmly welcome them.”
RFA attempted to contact Khaing Khaing Soe, spokesperson for the military government’s presidential office, but received no reply.
Col. Saw Kyaw Nyunt, spokesperson for the 7 EAO Alliance of ethnic armed organizations that have individually signed a Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement with the military, said the shift in U.S. attitude might be due to an understanding of Myanmar’s needs.
“In attempting to restart the peace process, international support and assistance are needed. The shift in attitude by the U.S. toward the peace process is likely because they realized that peace is urgently needed due to Myanmar’s reality. By 2030, which is in three or four years, seeking ways to build sustainable peace during that period can be viewed as assessing and speaking on our country’s needs.”
Salai Shein Tun, a secretariat member of the Chin National League for Democracy Party, which won a single seat in Myanmar’s parliament in the 2020 general election, told RFA that the new U.S. policy might face challenges from competitors.
“Speaking of challenges, the challenge from China as a big power is strong. Inside Myanmar and within ethnic regions, the challenge is also strong. In areas bordering neighboring China, they approach with a Chinese style model, whereas looking at the western side, in Chin, Kachin, and Rakhine states, they emphasize federalism. The country they connect with is India … Areas connected with neighboring China do not talk about federalism. Discussions will take quite a bit of effort when those following the Chinese model want to negotiate with the domestic groups that follow the federal model.”
According to the Integrated Country Strategy document, the released text was approved by the Trump administration on Aug. 31, 2026, before the mid-September secret visit to Naypyidaw by Michael Vance, the assistant secretary of state for intelligence and research.
Vance also led at least 12 U.S. government officials during a second round of talks with Myanmar military government officials in Tokyo in the second week of October.
Edited by Eugene Whong.
Update includes comments from Saw Kler Say.

articles.title: Top Uni presidents forum opens
articles.excerpt: The World Class University Presidents Forum 2026 opened today on the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology campus. The…
articles.fullText:
The World Class University Presidents Forum 2026 opened today on the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology campus.

The two-day forum, themed “Higher Education Reimagined: Innovating for the Future”, brings together in Hong Kong presidents and senior leadership figures from around 50 world-leading universities to explore strategic directions for the development of global higher education.

As a premier event in the global education community fully supported by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government and hosted by the HKUST, the forum highlights Hong Kong’s unique strengths and its pivotal status as a bridge connecting the Chinese Mainland with the global higher education system.

Officiating at the opening ceremony, Acting Chief Executive Chan Kwok-ki noted in his speech that higher education has long been a vital pillar of Hong Kong’s success and a cornerstone of its role as a hub for global talent and academic exchange.

He highlighted that Hong Kong is the only city in the world to host five universities in the global top 100 – a testament to the strength of its higher education sector, which is further underscored by the latest QS World University Rankings: Asia 2027.

The Hong Kong SAR Government will continue to align closely with national strategies, accelerate the integrated development of education, technology and talent, and further consolidate Hong Kong’s status as an international hub for post-secondary education through initiatives such as the development of the Northern Metropolis University Town.

Several heavyweight interuniversity co-operation signing ceremonies took place during the event, marking important strategic co-operation agreements between leading institutions and organisations at home and abroad. These included a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on deepening collaboration between Central South University and Monash University; an MOU between Zhejiang University and the HKUST on establishing a joint innovation centre; a Trilateral Joint Seed Fund agreement among the University of Warwick, Nanyang Technological University and Shanghai Jiao Tong University; and a student exchange agreement between Trinity College Dublin and Nanjing University, marking a new milestone in global higher education and research collaborative innovation.

Today’s topics include “The University and the Century Ahead”, “Educating the Human: The Generation Shaping the Intelligent Age”, and “From Ideas to Innovation: Universities Driving the Future Economy”.

A number of prominent leaders from the political, business and academic sectors addressed the forum either in person or via video message, including the eighth Secretary-General of the United Nations Ban Ki-moon, President of the 43rd session of the General Conference of UNESCO Khondker M Talha, President of the China Association of Higher Education Lin Huiqing, HKUST Council Chairman Harry Shum, and HKUST President Nancy Ip.

articles.title: Analysts: China could erode Taiwan’s hold on remote Pratas Island without invasion
articles.excerpt: Restricting supplies could give Beijing leverage, but forcing a withdrawal would risk a wider crisis.
articles.fullText:
China could cut off supplies to Taiwan-controlled Pratas Island, but forcing Taipei to abandon the remote outpost would require a sustained operation that might be too risky for Beijing, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
The tiny atoll known as Dongsha Island in Chinese lies more than 400 kilometers (250 miles) from Taiwan’s main island, about 260 kilometers (160 miles) from the Chinese mainland in the northern South China Sea.
The island’s isolation makes maintaining access by sea and air central to sustaining the coast guard and military personnel stationed there.
Beijing likely has the power to cut Pratas off completely, but such a move might not be necessary at all, Benjamin Blandin, a maritime security expert and visiting research fellow at Taiwan’s Institute for National Defense and Security Research, told RFA.
“China could achieve significant strategic benefits without imposing a complete blockade or forcing an immediate Taiwanese withdrawal,” said Blandin.
For Beijing, the potential gains could include regulating selected activities or compelling Taiwan to negotiate access, Blandin said. Such restrictions could erode Taipei’s authority even while Taiwanese personnel remained on the island.
A map showing the location of Taiwan-controlled Pratas Island in the northern South China Sea.
(RFA) But disrupting deliveries and making the outpost impossible to sustain are different objectives, Sylwia M. Gorska, a doctoral candidate in international relations at Britain’s University of Central Lancashire, told RFA.
“Making Taiwan’s presence unsustainable would require much more extensive restrictions, particularly given the island’s existing air and maritime supply options,” Gorska told RFA.
The portion of the atoll above sea level features an air strip and two piers.
Both analysts cautioned that recent encounters near Pratas do not establish that Beijing has decided to cut the island off, though these encounters have sharpened concerns about access.
Posturing coast guards
Taiwan’s coast guard on Sunday accused China of “harassment” after a Chinese coast guard ship on Saturday went into a restricted area of water near the atoll. A Taiwan coast guard vessel got as close as 1 nautical mile and asked the Chinese ship to leave.
Taipei called on China to “immediately cease” its acts of harassment, after what it said was the 13th such incursion near Pratas Island this year.
China maintains that the atoll is within its sovereign territory and called the incident a “routine law enforcement patrol.”
It was the third Pratas-related incident between the two countries in October alone, with similar incidents occurring Oct. 18 and Oct. 1.
A Taiwan coast guard patrol vessel, right, sailing near a China coast guard ship in waters south of Kinmen, Taiwan, July 8, 2026.
(Taiwan Coast Guard/AFP) Such encounters challenge Taiwan’s authority, the analysts said, but the more consequential test would involve Chinese ships issuing instructions to Taiwanese supply missions, then enforcing compliance.
Blandin identified three potentially overlapping stages: normalizing China’s maritime presence, asserting jurisdiction, and establishing effective control over access.
Demands for identification, inspections or course changes would indicate a move toward exercising authority, he said, adding that repeated obstruction of deliveries, personnel rotations or emergency evacuations would provide stronger evidence of an isolation campaign.
“The distinction between challenging Taiwan’s maritime authority and actively preventing the replenishment of its outposts is fundamental,” Blandin said.
Gorska said requirements for advance authorization or compulsory inspections would signal an attempt to regulate access. Persistent obstruction of successive deliveries, particularly alongside interference with flights, would indicate a more extensive effort to isolate Pratas.
“The principal concern is that Beijing may eventually seek to enforce the authority it is currently asserting, thereby transforming jurisdictional claims into restrictions on access,” she said.
Keeping supplies moving
Taiwan has strengthened its local patrol capabilities. Its coast guard said in September that a wharf renovation had been completed on July 1, allowing newly built 100-ton patrol boats to be stationed at Pratas alongside regular deployments of larger patrol ships nearby.
Those improvements strengthen the response around the atoll but do not guarantee security along its supply routes, Gorska said.
Larger reserves would give Taiwan more time to respond to disrupted deliveries, while maintaining maritime and air transport would provide flexibility. Blandin said sea transport would remain important for substantial quantities of equipment and provisions, with aircraft offering a complementary option when conditions permitted.
The outpost at Pratas atoll, as of Oct. 4, 2020.
(Planet Labs) Escorting deliveries could help preserve access, but repeated Chinese obstructions would force difficult decisions about how far Taiwan should go to challenge them.
Taipei could deploy additional coast guard vessels, improve surveillance or involve military assets more directly, Blandin said. Each option would have to be weighed against the risk of escalation.
“Beijing’s main challenge would be sustaining those restrictions without losing control over the level of confrontation,” Gorska said.
Stopping an individual delivery leaves room to retreat or negotiate, she said. Repeatedly preventing escorted ships or aircraft from reaching Pratas would carry substantially greater risks and could provoke a wider cross-Strait crisis.
Lessons from the Philippines
The Philippines’ efforts to supply its outpost aboard the grounded BRP Sierra Madre at Second Thomas Shoal offer a comparison, although the geography, logistical needs and security arrangements differ.
Blandin said Manila’s persistence in continuing deliveries, along with documenting and publicizing confrontations, offered lessons for Taiwan. Defensive equipment, surveillance and proportionate responses could improve resilience, but none would guarantee access against sustained interference.
Gorska said practical arrangements to prevent dangerous encounters also carried a political challenge: communication should not become an acceptance of Beijing’s claimed authority to approve deliveries.
A Taiwanese coast guard handles a machine gun at a fort on the Pratas Islands in the South China Sea in a file photo from January 2000.
(Reuters) The comparison has another major limit. The Philippines has a mutual defense treaty with Washington, and U.S. defense guidelines explicitly include armed attacks on Philippine coast guard vessels in the South China Sea within those commitments. Taiwan has no equivalent treaty.
The Taiwan Relations Act treats efforts to determine Taiwan’s future through nonpeaceful means, including boycotts or embargoes, as a matter of grave concern to the United States. It does not specify a U.S. military response to interference with supplies to Pratas.
That uncertainty would factor into Beijing’s calculations, Gorska said.
For Blandin, China’s ability to deploy ships around Pratas is only the beginning.
“The central question is therefore not simply whether China possesses the capabilities to isolate Pratas, but whether it could sustain such an operation and convert maritime coercion into lasting territorial control at an acceptable political, military and diplomatic cost.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: 5 HK universities in Asia's top 10
articles.excerpt: The Education Bureau said today that Hong Kong’s higher education institutions had delivered a stellar performance in the “World University…
articles.fullText:
The Education Bureau said today that Hong Kong’s higher education institutions had delivered a stellar performance in the “World University Rankings: Asia 2027” published by Quacquarelli Symonds (QS), an international higher education research organisation.

The bureau said that overall the sector had once again demonstrated outstanding international competitiveness and academic excellence within Asia.

It added that the results reflect the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government’s sustained commitment to investing resources and its proactive initiatives in supporting higher education development, which have consolidated the city’s position as an international post-secondary education hub.

In the latest rankings, the University of Hong Kong retained the top spot in Asia.

A total of five Hong Kong universities are among Asia’s top 10, with three of these ranking in the top five: besides the University of Hong Kong, City University of Hong Kong ranked fourth, with the Chinese University of Hong Kong sitting in fifth.

Eight local universities improved their rankings this year, with all 11 ranked Hong Kong institutions featuring among the top 500 in Asia. The bureau said this demonstrates a comprehensive elevation in the quality of Hong Kong’s higher education.

At the same time, Hong Kong universities continue to lead Asia in key indicators such as academic reputation, employer reputation, internationalisation, and research impact.

The bureau also highlighted that the World Class University Presidents Forum 2026 will be inaugurated tomorrow.

A premier international education event, the forum brings together university presidents, distinguished scholars, and international education leaders from dozens of world-class institutions to deliberate on issues such as talent cultivation in the intelligent era, the role of technology and innovation in driving the future economy, and universities’ responses to major global challenges.

The Hong Kong SAR Government said it will continue to support local universities in reaching new heights and enhance the international leadership of Hong Kong’s higher education sector through various policies and measures. These include advancing the development of the Northern Metropolis University Town, attracting top international research talent and students, and deepening cross-boundary and international academic collaborations.

articles.title: Telling infrastructure stories well
articles.excerpt: Jointly launched by the Development Bureau and the Construction Industry Council, the “Hong Kong Infrastructure NO. 1” campaign seeks to…
articles.fullText:
Jointly launched by the Development Bureau and the Construction Industry Council, the “Hong Kong Infrastructure NO. 1” campaign seeks to deepen public understanding of the city’s infrastructure projects.

Through guided tours, interactive workshops, exhibitions and tailored teaching materials, the campaign shares professional engineering knowledge in an engaging and accessible way, allowing young people to explore careers in the construction industry.

Awe-inspiring visit
A group of primary school pupils toured the education centre at Plant Number 3 of the Kai Tak District Cooling System, where they learnt about the climate challenges facing Hong Kong and how the cooling system works.

Interactive exhibits helped the pupils understand the technology behind the system, while a tour of the plant’s core facilities gave them a close-up view of its large-scale machinery and extensive network of pipes.

The facility completely defied the expectations of Primary 5 pupil Horace Tang.

“I was amazed by the sheer size of the plant and its enormous pipes,” he said.

“I think the district cooling system is remarkable because it helps reduce carbon emissions and save energy. The tour has inspired me to become an engineer in the future.”

Hands-on learning
The initiative focuses on three key areas: education, public engagement and media promotion.

On the education front, the campaign organises guided tours and engineering visits, while also providing a dedicated resource centre, interactive workshops and tailored learning and teaching materials.

The construction-themed materials integrate science, technology, engineering, the arts and mathematics, allowing students to explore subjects such as urban planning in an engaging and practical manner.

Moving beyond classroom concepts, students actively design their own communities within strict special limits and specific guidelines.

Secondary 3 pupil Chui Ki-hin said the workshop transformed his understanding of urban planning.

“I used to think urban planning was simple - that you could just arrange buildings like building blocks and connect the necessary utilities,” he said.

“However, after taking part in the workshop, I realised that it is much more complicated and that there are many constraints to consider.”

Even producing a small model required considerable thought and effort.

“It took me about 45 minutes just to complete this small model. I can only imagine how much more challenging it is to plan a real city.”

International recognition
Apart from its education initiatives, the campaign reaches the community through videos, social media content, exhibitions, quizzes and other public engagement activities.

The campaign’s impact has resonated far beyond Hong Kong. At the 23rd International Business Awards, the promotional initiative triumphed across 10 different categories - capturing six Gold and three Silver awards, as well as one Bronze.

“The aim is to use interesting and heartfelt stories to help the public more easily understand the advanced technologies adopted in infrastructure projects that we see in everyday life, and appreciate the craftsmanship spirit of our construction industry professionals,” Principal Assistant Secretary for Development (Works) Chris Ng said.

He added that Hong Kong’s global standing in engineering would not be possible without the commitment and expertise of industry professionals.

Construction Industry Council General Manager - Corporate Communications Hanks Lee said the trickiest part of the campaign was figuring out how to share professional engineering know-how in a down-to-earth and lively way.

“With the wholehearted support of the industry providing invaluable experience, practical examples and on-site assistance, we were able to tell the story of Hong Kong’s infrastructure.”

Looking ahead, the Development Bureau will continue to leverage digital and innovative media to showcase the technological advancement and professionalism of the construction industry. Through these efforts, it aims to deepen public understanding of the vital role infrastructure plays in Hong Kong’s economic, social and livelihood development, while attracting more young people to join the industry and carry forward the spirit of striving for excellence.

articles.title: U.S. to China after demolition report: ‘End interference in Tibetan religious life’
articles.excerpt: Demolition of monks’ quarters aimed at reducing their population and making assimilation easier, sources tell RFA.
articles.fullText:
The U.S. government Thursday urged China to stop interfering with Tibetan religious freedom after sources in eastern Tibet told Radio Free Asia that Chinese authorities began demolishing monks’ quarters at a monastery there.
Authorities on Oct. 25 and 26 began demolishing about 200 monks’ residences at Dza Sershul Thekchen Dargyeling Monastery in Sershul County in the Kardze (Ganzi in Chinese) Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, sources there told RFA, speaking on the condition of anonymity for security reasons.
“Everything is over now,” the source said. “We are losing everything.”
A U.S. State Department spokesperson told RFA on Thursday that the demolitions in Sershul reflect broader Chinese government efforts to bring spiritual institutions, religious education, and monastic life under government control.
“We call on Beijing to end its interference in Tibetan religious life,” the spokesperson said. “Tibetan Buddhists should have the right to practice their faith freely, educate their clergy and choose their religious leaders, including the Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama, without government interference,” the spokesperson said, referring to Beijing’s past and likely future interference with the established succession customs of the two most important figures in Tibetan Buddhism.
The demolition in Sershul is not isolated, but part of a larger campaign to reduce monk populations at Tibetan religious institutions. RFA reported in August that authorities resumed demolition of the Larung Gar Buddhist Academy. Activists noted the timing – China’s new Ethnic Unity and Progress Law – had just come into effect the previous month.
The law focuses on reshaping ethnic identity, changing the legal framework around language, expanding state oversight of religion, and extending the law’s reach beyond China’s border.
Dza Sershul Thekchen Dargyeling Monastery in an undated photo.
(Citizen photo) The source in Tibet said that authorities are planning further restrictions that would prevent monks from staying at the monastery after the demolitions.
“Tibetan religion and culture are being destroyed,” the source told RFA, adding that there is little recourse for those opposed to the demolitions.
“No matter how much local people speak out, the authorities do not listen,” the source said. “They do not remember, they ignore us. We have no solutions and we don’t know what will happen.”
RFA contacted the relevant county-level officials in Sershul for comment, but the official who answered the phone did not respond to RFA’s questions and hung up.
Promoting “ethnic unity”
The demolitions and reductions of the monk population are clearly intended to assimilate Tibetans so that they accept Chinese identity, Tenzin Lekshay, spokesperson for the Central Tibetan Administration, or CTA, the Tibetan government-in-exile based in Dharamsala, India, told RFA.
“This is a mask used by the Chinese government under the recently enacted Ethnic Unity Law to assimilate Tibetans and destroy Tibetan religion, culture, and language,” he said. “This is not the first time. We have also seen young monks forcibly expelled from monasteries and sent to China’s colonial boarding schools .”
Though Beijing claims the boarding schools are aimed at providing education to a scattered population, critics have noted that their actual goal is assimilation.
“We strongly condemn the Chinese government’s continued attempts to shut down monasteries and schools established by Tibetans while claiming its authority over Tibet and seeking to eradicate Tibetan national identity,” Tenzin Lekshay said. “It is time for the Chinese government to acknowledge and trust that Tibetan religion and culture are beneficial to China and the world and that the destruction of Tibetan religion and culture will have negative consequences for both China and the world.”
He said that the Chinese government’s actions, which violate international law, would undermine Beijing’s ambition to establish itself as a global leader.
The entrance to Dza Sershul Thekchen Dargyeling Monastery in an undated photo.
(Citizen photo) Tibetan monasteries are central to preserving Tibetan culture and religious identity, Sangay Kyab, Chinese liaison officer at the Tibet Bureau, the CTA’s representative office in Geneva, Switzerland, told RFA.
“Tibetan culture and religion are central to the identity of the Tibetan people. China’s policy and goal is to destroy everything that keeps Tibet alive,” he said. “Since China invaded Tibet, there have been successive campaigns against Tibetan monasteries, often under the pretext of reforming them.”
He explained how monks and nuns are subjected to political education aimed at making monasteries conform to the Chinese Communist Party’s ideology.
“The main goal is to restrict the study and practice of Tibetan Buddhism and undermine the Tibetan people’s ability to unite,” he said. “The incident at the monastery is connected to the Chinese government’s broader policies toward Tibet, and there is a risk that similar incidents could occur elsewhere,” he said.
Restrictions in Tibet threaten Tibetan Buddhist heritage, warned the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, an independent, bipartisan U.S. government commission that monitors religious freedom abroad and makes policy recommendations to the U.S. government.
“Demolition of Tibetan monasteries is just one tactic in a wider effort by Chinese authorities to sever the people of Tibet from their Tibetan Buddhist heritage, including the forced assimilation of ethnic minorities through the draconian ‘Ethnic Unity’ law that came into effect in July,” commission chair Asif Mahmood told RFA.
He cited the resumption of demolition at Larung Gar in Sichuan province in July as another example of restrictions on Tibetan Buddhist religious freedom.
“Buddhist monks in these circumstances have faced persistent threats of harassment, expulsion from their monasteries, imprisonment, and worse,” he said.
China is trying to destroy Tibetan Buddhism at its roots, Bhuchung K. Tsering, head of the Research and Monitoring Unit at the Washington-based International Campaign for Tibet, told RFA.
“Monasteries across Tibet are required to follow the orders of the Chinese Communist Party and serve its objectives,” he said. “The Chinese government claims that Tibetans enjoy freedom of religion, but the reality is the opposite of its claims that it is promoting Tibetan Buddhism,” he added.
Translation and additional reporting by Tenzin Dickyi, edited by Tawang for RFA Tibetan. Edited by Eugene Whong for RFA English.

articles.title: China leverages Taiwan’s reverence for Sun Yat-sen to promote ‘reunification’
articles.excerpt: Shared history fosters cross-strait kinship, but analysts say China’s framing sways only those already pro-Beijing.
articles.fullText:
Beijing is trying to use national hero Sun Yat-sen – who is also revered in Taiwan – to frame “reunification” with the democratic island as the fulfillment of a common national destiny, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
Ahead of the 160th anniversary of Sun’s birth on Nov. 12, the mainland has planned official commemorations, and Taiwan’s government warned that Beijing was using the revolutionary leader’s legacy to further an “ anti-independence, pro-reunification ” strategy.
Taiwan considers Sun to be the “father of the country.” He helped lead the revolution that ended China’s imperial system and became the Republic of China’s first provisional president in 1912. The government of the Republic of China fled to Taiwan in 1949 when Chiang Kai-shek’s nationalists lost the Chinese Civil War to Mao Zedong’s communists. Taiwan still uses “Republic of China” as its official name.
In Beijing’s view, Sun is the “forerunner of the revolution.” Mao is considered to have continued in his footsteps, and the communist “People’s Republic of China” is said to be the realization of Sun’s unfinished vision. It is this version of history that China wants to push, Jozef Huljak, a political science doctoral candidate at Constantine the Philosopher University in Slovakia whose research examines Taiwan’s cultural and public diplomacy, told RFA.
“In my view, Beijing’s core strategy is a battle over words: if the world accepts its version of history, a takeover can be sold as ‘reunification,’” Huljak said.
Soldiers stand in front of a Taiwan flag and a portrait of Sun Yat-sen, the founding father of the Republic of China, after Taiwan’s military demonstrated combat readiness ahead of the upcoming Lunar New Year holidays in an annual exercise in Hsinchu, Taiwan, Jan. 7, 2025.
(Ann Wang/Reuters) Though China’s communist government has never governed Taiwan, it considers the democratic island to be a rogue province. It claims the island as its territory and has not renounced using force to bring it under Beijing’s control.
In addition to diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan, China’s historical messaging promotes a national belonging intended to make political union appear both legitimate and inevitable.
China’s own policy documents describe history and culture as forces driving unification. A 2022 white paper on Taiwan presented national unity as a longstanding Chinese aspiration and tied its achievement to the country’s national rejuvenation.
Sun as a political tool
Sun’s connection to China’s Taiwan policy is explicit. Beijing organized the cross-strait Sun Yat-sen Forum in his ancestral birthplace in June, and about 1,300 Taiwanese participants attended.
At that event, Pan Xianzhang, a deputy head of China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, urged people on both sides to draw inspiration from Sun while adhering to the “one-China principle,” Beijing’s doctrine that asserts Taiwan is an inalienable part of China.
“Beijing’s use of Sun works because Taipei still props him up,” Huljak said.
But the same historical figure can carry different political meanings. During an April visit to Sun’s mausoleum in Nanjing, Cheng Li-wun, chairperson of Taiwan’s main opposition Kuomintang, or KMT, – the Nationalist party founded by Sun – invoked his legacy to advocate reconciliation and dialogue. She also pointed to Taiwan’s democratic development as an expression of his founding principles.
Cheng Li-wun, chairperson of the Kuomintang, Taiwan's largest opposition party, speaks upon visiting Sun Yat-sen's Mausoleum in Nanjing, China April 8, 2026.
(via REUTERS) The KMT’s own account of the visit emphasized the continuation of Sun’s ideals in Taiwan and the promotion of peaceful cross-strait relations.
A broader repertoire
Sun’s birth anniversary is part of a wider pattern in which Chinese authorities connect history to a shared national identity and political unity with Taiwan.
Another figure honored on both sides of the strait is Zheng Chenggong, also known as Koxinga, who expelled the Dutch from Taiwan in 1662 and established a regime there. Beijing describes him as a national hero who recovered Chinese territory.
But in Taiwan the way Zheng is remembered depends on who you ask. For some, he is seen as analogous to Chiang Kai-shek, as both were military leaders who lost their respective campaigns on the mainland, fled to Taiwan, and vowed to return. To others, he is seen as having established a kingdom on Taiwan independent from mainland control.
The Portrait of Koxinga—a mid-17th century hanging scroll exhibited in the National Palace Museum in Taiwan
(National Palace Museum via Wikimedia Commons) In September 2024, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office highlighted commemorations marking the 400th anniversary of Zheng’s birth alongside exhibitions about families separated by the Taiwan Strait.
The two sides also frame the end of World War II differently.
In October 2025, China’s legislature designated Oct. 25 as a day commemorating what it calls Taiwan’s recovery from Japanese rule in 1945. The decision described that event as an important link in the historical and legal basis for Taiwan belonging to China.
But in Taiwan’s view, it was the Republic of China authorities who took over Taiwan’s administration after Japan’s surrender in 1945. The People’s Republic of China was founded four years later and has never ruled Taiwan.
Huljak said these competing interpretations of history and historical figures matter internationally as well as within Taiwan. In his assessment, acceptance of Beijing’s historical vocabulary can help normalize its present-day claims among foreign audiences unfamiliar with the distinction.
Symbols and their limits
The challenge for Beijing is that Taiwan’s identity has diverged since the Chinese civil war, the analysts said.
Under Chiang Kai-shek, the KMT claimed to represent all of China and ruled Taiwan through an authoritarian system. Martial law ended in 1987, and the island held its first direct presidential election in 1996, establishing a democratic basis for political authority.
President Chiang Kai-shek of Nationalist China delivers an address at a city hall reception in Taipei, March 2, 1950.
(Spencer Mosa/AP) That transformation helps explain the gap analysts see between Sun Yat-sen’s institutional prominence and his emotional relevance to many people in Taiwan.
“Claiming to be the true inheritor of Sun’s legacy is one of many similar methods Beijing uses to court Taiwanese and try to forge common bonds, but these claims have limited currency among a people for whom Sun has limited emotional resonance,” Sasha B. Chhabra, a Taiwan-based security analyst and publisher of the Formosa Review newsletter, told RFA.
Chhabra said Sun remained particularly important to KMT supporters in Taiwan, who prefer engagement with the mainland over independence. Huljak also identified KMT supporters and potential swing voters as audiences Beijing hoped to reach.
Neither assessment, however, establishes that commemorations change political preferences. Shared respect for a historical figure can provide an opening for contact without producing agreement over sovereignty or support for Communist rule.
For Chhabra, figures associated with Taiwan’s own political development have greater relevance to many residents than the revolutionary founder honored by both governments.
“Taiwanese are more interested in commemorating figures with a tangible legacy in the country, such as presidents Lee Teng-hui or Chiang Jing-kuo,” he said, referring to Taiwan’s first directly elected president and his predecessor, who lifted martial law in 1987.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Wang Fuk Court fire report released
articles.excerpt: (To watch the full press conference with sign language interpretation, click here .) Chief Executive John Lee today announced that…
articles.fullText:
(To watch the full press conference with sign language interpretation, click here .)

Chief Executive John Lee today announced that the Government will launch comprehensive reforms following the release of the independent committee’s report on the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po.

The blaze resulted in the deaths of 168 people, including a fireman who died in the line of duty. At a press conference unveiling the report, Mr Lee and principal officials bowed in apology for the pain and sorrow caused to the affected families and the community.

Addressing political accountability, Mr Lee announced that Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho had tendered her resignation. He has made a submission to the Central People's Government, recommending her removal from the post.

“Considering that the fire took place in Wang Fuk Court and it falls within the purview of the Independent Checking Unit, which is under the Housing Bureau, the Secretary for Housing should take political accountability.

“I also set two requirements for my political team. First, continue in their respective positions to exert the utmost efforts amidst the reforms and the substantial amount of work ahead.

“Second, learn from the incident, strengthen leadership and pursue more vigorously result-oriented governance,” he said.

With effect from today, Ms Ho's duties as the Secretary for Housing are suspended. Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong has concurrently assumed the post of Acting Secretary for Housing.

The Government received the independent committee’s report last Thursday. After seeking legal advice, parts of the report have been redacted to prevent any actual or perceived undue prejudice to ongoing criminal prosecutions.

The report highlighted that the rapid spread of the fire and the high number of casualties were caused by the suspected substitution of fire-retardant scaffolding nets with non-fire-retardant ones, the use of non-fire-retardant foam boards and other flammable materials during the works, as well as the creation of access openings in the escape staircases for convenience.

It also pointed out that the long-standing regulatory system for building maintenance and renovation relies heavily on the integrity and professional conduct of industry professionals and contractors. However, certain individuals are suspected of abandoning their supervisory and management responsibilities, rendering oversight effectively non-existent.

Deficiencies and failings were detailed across relevant government departments, including the Independent Checking Unit under the Housing Bureau, the Buildings Department, the Fire Services Department and the Labour Department.

Furthermore, the report noted that because building maintenance and renovation projects involve substantial sums of money, they have become targets for triads and criminals. These groups have formed syndicates to rig bids and monopolise the market through intimidation, fraud and corruption.

The independent committee put forward 120 recommendations in its report, which has been published online for public viewing.

Noting that bid-rigging is the root cause of the problems, that the Mandatory Building Inspection Scheme has deficiencies, and that property owners lack the professional knowledge to protect themselves from fraud, Mr Lee said the Government will implement comprehensive and systemic reform .

The Government will legislate against bid-rigging in building maintenance and renovation projects, establish a cross-departmental task force to combat relevant crimes, and set up a Building Maintenance Support & Services Council.

Additionally, the Government will overhaul the operational and regulatory system for building works, restructure regulatory departments, establish a centralised data system and reform the complaint mechanism.

“In addition to the 120 recommendations, we will do more – such as revamping the complaints system, ensuring that complaints are not just handled at departmental level but will be upgraded to the central system, with senior officials in the centre using assistive artificial intelligence to identify repeated problems, to identify probable complaints we do not think are handled to the best degree as we would like,” Mr Lee said.

A steering committee led by the Chief Secretary will be set up to review each recommendation, drive implementation and monitor the submission of proposed legislative amendments across six pieces of legislation to the Legislative Council.

Separately, the Chief Executive has activated the Administrative Responsibility Two-tier Investigation Mechanism under the Heads of Department Accountability System. The case has been referred to the Public Service Commission to conduct an investigation into the alleged deficiencies and failings of the civil servants concerned. The probe is expected to be completed within three months.

The Government added that the full report will be released after all relevant criminal proceedings have concluded.

articles.title: Shenzhen Bay to extend hours
articles.excerpt: The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government today announced that passenger and vehicle clearance services at the Shenzhen Bay Control…
articles.fullText:
The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government today announced that passenger and vehicle clearance services at the Shenzhen Bay Control Point will be extended by two hours until 2am on October 30 and 31. The arrangement follows a consensus reached with Shenzhen authorities to facilitate festival traffic.

A substantial rise in visitor arrivals and late-night cross-boundary trips is anticipated over the Halloween weekend, which coincides with major local events including the Hong Kong Wine & Dine Festival and mega concerts.

The Hong Kong SAR Government expects the busiest period for northbound traffic at Huanggang Port to be between 11pm and 2am overnight, warning of heavy congestion around the port area and San Tin Highway. The extended hours at Shenzhen Bay aim to divert this late-night flow.

Cross-boundary coach operators have co-ordinated with the Hong Kong SAR Government to extend northbound services utilizing the Shenzhen Bay Control Point.

For local public transport services, franchised bus operators will run two special overnight bus routes – NB2 and NB3 – during the early morning hours. These will connect the Shenzhen Bay Control Point and Yuen Long/Tin Shui Wai and Tuen Mun respectively.

Clearance arrangements at Huanggang Port will remain unchanged.

Travellers are advised to check real-time updates – including average passenger and private car waiting times – via the Security Bureau’s “Easy Boundary” platform or the Transport Department’s “HKeMobility” mobile application to plan their journeys and avoid delays.

articles.title: South China Sea tensions cause China to ‘recall’ teachers from the Philippines
articles.excerpt: Experts caution against xenophobia, but point to links between educational exchange and advocacy of China’s claims.
articles.fullText:
South China Sea tensions are turning Chinese-language education into a security issue in the Philippines, straining civilian ties and exposing schools’ dependence on foreign teaching support, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
At the beginning of this month, reports surfaced that around 150 teachers, mostly instructors of Mandarin Chinese who worked in schools that serve the Philippines’ Chinoy , or ethnic Chinese, communities, were returning to China after Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and other officials cautioned that educational exchanges with Beijing could potentially lead to national security threats.
The exodus was the result of the teachers’ families requesting that they return to China according to the Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, a commercial organization serving ethnic Chinese communities in the Philippines. The federation and the Chinese Embassy approved the requests.
In a report on the SeaLight webpage , the maritime transparency project’s executive director Ray Powell characterized the exodus as an organized recall by Beijing that uses “Filipinos of Chinese heritage” as “a card to be played.”
China and the Philippines have become increasingly at odds over their territorial disputes in the South China Sea, and Beijing has been known to use “gray zone” tactics – pressure that can include anything except armed conflict – to advance its claims.
“China’s gray-zone pressure at sea and its political warfare ashore are intertwined, and this episode shows the connective tissue,” Powell told RFA.
The number of affected teachers could be higher than initially disclosed. China’s Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan put it closer to 180 while delivering an address to the 20th anniversary celebration of the Confucius Institute at Ateneo de Manila University.
China's Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan addresses the 20th anniversary celebration of the Confucius Institute at Ateneo de Manila University Oct. 13, 2026.
(Embassy of the People's Republic of China in the Republic of the Philippines) Jing also rejected allegations that Chinese-language education amounted to political infiltration, calling them “baseless and absurd.”
But Powell said in his report that he and Teodoro had concerns about China-linked education programs being tied to China’s United Front Work Department – the strategy and network by which Beijing projects its political influence overseas.
Reports and rhetoric
Maritime confrontation provided the backdrop, while specific developments involving a Chinese university helped trigger the scrutiny of the programs, Aniello Iannone, a lecturer in international relations and general secretary of the ASEAN Studies Center at Indonesia’s President University, told RFA.
“The spark came from a university symposium and a think-tank report,” he told RFA.
Iannone was referring to the symposium hosted in late June at Jinan University in Guangzhou, China, where scholars advanced a claim that Batanes, the Philippines’ northernmost province, belonged to China through Taiwan .
In July, Powell published a report on the SeaLight website that provided evidence linking Jinan University to training teachers for Chinese-language schools in the Philippines – 43 of 56 Filipino teacher trainees sent to China in 2024 through the Philippine Chinese Education Research Center, he said in the report.
The Filipino trainees were not the mainland Chinese teachers who were recalled, Powell told RFA.
“I haven’t found these programs directly teaching Beijing’s South China Sea claims, and I won’t allege it,” he said.
Instead, he argued that affiliated organizations can support Beijing’s objectives through broader political messaging, including appeals for peace and dialogue that he interprets as encouraging acceptance of Chinese pressure at sea.
Powell views the teacher recall as political pressure that directs anger over disrupted lessons toward Beijing’s critics. But he said he had not seen the teachers’ return linked to any Philippine concession over the South China Sea.
Iannone said the available evidence required more careful distinctions.
“Before acting, authorities should separate a structural link, such as who trained a teacher, from conduct, such as what was taught, and publish what they find,” he said.
Lessons from the U.S. backlash
The controversy in the Philippines echoes concerns that drove a backlash against Confucius Institutes in the United States, but the mechanisms differ.
Confucius Institutes are Chinese government-backed partnerships with overseas universities that provide Chinese-language teaching and cultural programs. Their funding arrangements and ties to Beijing raised concerns in the United States about transparency, academic freedom and potential political influence on campuses.
A 2023 U.S. Government Accountability Office report found that the number of institutes at American universities and colleges had fallen from about 100 in 2019 to fewer than five today. Schools most commonly cited potential losses of federal funding and external pressure as contributing to closures. Many also reported reduced language-learning opportunities afterward.
Undergraduate student Moe Lewis, left, shows her watercolor painting of peony leaves at a traditional Chinese painting class at the Confucius Institute at George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, May 2, 2018.
(Matthew Pennington/AP) The Philippine teacher-placement programs involved in the recall are distinct from Confucius Institutes.
Iannone said the American experience can be seen primarily as a warning about how funding pressure and governance concerns can drive decisions even when allegations of misconduct remain unresolved.
He proposed a public register of educational agreements, funding and staffing covering every foreign government supporting Philippine education, alongside full local control over curriculum and hiring.
Funding alternatives would also be necessary, he said. Greater scrutiny alone would not solve schools’ dependence on overseas teachers.
“A more durable setup would train Filipino Mandarin teachers at home, draw on more than one partner – Taiwan included – and put every agreement on the public record,” he said.
Communities caught in the middle
The consequences could extend beyond disrupted classes.
Iannone warned that public debate could blur distinctions between Chinese state institutions, Chinese-language schools and people of Chinese heritage.
“What worries me more is how quickly the language slides, from PRC state bodies to ‘Chinese schools’ to ‘the Chinese,’” he said.
Teodoro, the most well-known Philippine government official who expressed concerns over the educational exchanges, prefaced them with a warning against xenophobia and said that the information the government had on the exchanges did not necessarily constitute wrongdoing.
A map showing the location of the five Confucius Institutes in the Philippines.
(RFA) But prolonged suspicion of China or Chinese could affect Filipinos who earned degrees in China, potentially damaging their careers if employers or institutions began treating their education as evidence of disloyalty,” Enrico Cau, a Taipei-based independent security researcher, told RFA.
He cautioned against assuming that changes in outlook after studying abroad necessarily resulted from organized political influence.
“Mindset shifts in those cases can result from spontaneous changes of mind, rather than from deliberate attempts to influence them,” he said.
Cau nevertheless considers a broad rupture unlikely. Educational exchanges form only one part of a relationship sustained by business networks, institutional connections and extensive personal ties, he said.
He described competing approaches within Philippine policy: a confrontational effort to check Chinese assertiveness and quieter diplomacy seeking to preserve economic and civilian relationships.
“These two souls seem to coexist in some way, producing a mix of constructive and dissonant results,” he said.
Powell said the recall could discourage oversight or prompt schools to seek different partners. He would not predict which outcome would prevail.
Iannone argued that preserving educational ties required arrangements able to withstand continued maritime confrontation.
“The influence concerns should be investigated properly, which means findings the public can actually read,” he said. “Otherwise the Philippines risks spending a great deal of political energy on Mandarin teachers while the harder problems at sea stay where they are.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Online post purportedly by Chinese students calls for restoring term limits for Xi
articles.excerpt: Letter appeared on website registered in South Korea with Singapore mailing address, RFA investigation reveals.
articles.fullText:
Updated on Oct. 27, 2026 at 3:45 p.m. ET
Read a version of this story in Chinese
An “open letter” purportedly signed by students from multiple Chinese universities appeared on a Chinese language website on Monday, calling for the restoration of term limits for the Chinese president, but an investigation by Radio Free Asia was not able to determine if it originated from within China.
The letter, which was no longer accessible on Tuesday, had also called for the promotion of democratic constitutional amendments and the guarantee of space for citizens to discuss national affairs, appeared the same day as the opening of the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, or CCP.
RFA’s investigation revealed that the “Siyuan Lake BBS” website hosting the message listed “KR” as its country/region code, indicating South Korea, in its registration information. Its mailing address was listed as “16 Collyer Quay,” a skyscraper in Singapore’s central business district. The administrator’s email address was registered on a server of Chinese tech giant Tencent.
Based on the above information, RFA was unable to determine whether the Chinese language website is located within China. As for which organization or company manages it, this cannot be verified at present.
A Radio Free Asia investigation revealed the website to be registered to a Singapore address in South Korea.
(ICANN Lookup) The “open letter,” posted at 3:18 p.m., was titled “A Joint Appeal from a Group of University Students in the Republic.” It was addressed to the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China, the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress, and members of the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, and was written against the backdrop of commemorating the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen, the founder of modern China at the end of its last imperial dynasty.
The article cites past statements by Sun Yat-sen, Mao Zedong, and Deng Xiaoping regarding democracy, oversight of power, and leadership systems, and questions China’s 2018 constitutional amendment that removed the two-term limit for the president and vice president, paving the way for Xi’s third term as president, which began in 2023.
The letter argues that political stability should stem from predictability in the system and advocates for “limiting the time limit on power and subjecting it to oversight.”
Three Main Demands
The open letter put forward three main expectations:
Restore Term Limits: Abolish the indefinite extension of the term of office for the President of the People’s Republic of China and restore the term limits explicitly stipulated in the Constitution to ensure the orderly transfer of power; clear term limits should also be established for the highest leadership positions of the Party.
Initiate Democratic Constitutional Amendment: Convene a national constitutional amendment conference, steadily and gradually expand the people’s substantive participation in public power, improve the election, supervision, and recall mechanisms, and put into practice the unfinished goal since the 1911 Xinhai Revolution—returning power to the people—step by step.
Safeguard Space for Public Discussion: Safeguard the space for citizens to discuss national affairs in accordance with the law, encourage young people of the Republic to speak the truth, and listen to criticism as well-intentioned suggestions.
The article also states:
“We have no intention of confrontation, much less to create antagonism. We are just a group of young people who grew up reading Dr. Sun Yat-sen’s last words, and with the sentiment that ‘the revolution has not yet succeeded, comrades must continue to strive,’ we are willing to fulfill the responsibility of a scholar for the long-term future of this country.”
Unverified signatures and origin
The post lists 14 universities, including Peking University, Renmin University of China, Tongji University, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xiamen University, and Nankai University, and notes that the petition is ongoing. However, the list only includes the names of the universities and does not provide any individual signatures or proof of signature.
An online post on Oct. 26, 2026, purportedly by Chinese students calls for restoring term limits for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
(RFA Mandarin) As of midnight Beijing time on October 27, the website showed that this article had only been viewed by 656 people and received 1 like. The author on the page is listed as “Lin Ziyi,” with an account level of “LV.1.” The website indicates that this is “Lin Ziyi’s” first article. The article does not provide the names, number, contact information, or other verifiable information of the students who signed the article.
RFA has not independently confirmed the author’s identity, whether the signatories are indeed students, or whether students from the listed schools actually participated.
The website is divided into several topics, with the “Open Letter” posted in the “Complaints and Casual Chat” section. The website is entirely in simplified Chinese and appears to be a typical campus job search or lifestyle information website.
A closer look
The bottom of the page states that it is a “non-official campus forum,” and a closer look reveals that its URL ends with “.com” instead of the usual “.cn” which is China’s internet domain.
Radio Free Asia further investigated the website’s registration information and found that the IP address used by the website was “43.155.168.161”. Further verification with ICANN revealed that the website’s registration information showed the “country/region” code as “KR”, which corresponds to South Korea. The mailing address was listed as “16 Collyer Quay” in Singapore, but the administrator’s email address was registered on a Tencent server (@tencent.com), and the mobile phone number and WeChat account left by the administrator were also Chinese numbers.
A Radio Free Asia investigation revealed the website to be registered to a Singapore address in South Korea.
(ICANN Lookup) ‘Conscience of intellectuals’
While the authenticity of the petition remains to be verified, its content reflects the conscience of intellectuals, Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council Minister Chiu Chui-cheng said at the Legislative Yuan on Tuesday.
Chiu also recalled that as early as 2017, Chinese scholars had expressed their opposition to Xi Jinping’s disruption of the leadership succession system.
At that time, the Chinese scholars stated bluntly, “We, the intellectuals of mainland China, absolutely cannot accept this re-election,” referring to a provision that granted him a second term under conditions that would allow him to serve a third in 2023. They indicated that if the leadership succession system were undermined, 95% of Chinese intellectuals would oppose it.
However, Chiu said that as the CCP later established a “one-man rule” leadership structure, the mechanism for intellectuals to correct their mistakes has “completely disappeared.”
Edited by Charlie Dharapak and Eugene Whong.
Update adds Chiu’s comments to the Legislative Yuan and information about the website’s disappearance.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un’s unprecedented day-trip to China shatters Pyongyang’s Korean War myths
articles.excerpt: Visit to army memorial acknowledges China’s role in the war, downplayed by North Korea’s version of history.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s weekend visit to China over the newly completed New Yalu River Bridge was largely symbolic, and acknowledged a history that Pyongyang has downplayed for three generations, experts told Radio Free Asia.
North Korea is drawing closer to China and Russia while keeping the U.S. at arm’s length. Kim Jong Un’s one-day trip to China is the latest sign.
During Saturday’s unprecedented one-day car trip to Dandong, China, across the border from North Korea’s northwestern city of Sinuiju, Kim inspected a bus factory, met with high-ranking Chinese officials, and visited a monument that commemorated China’s entry into the Korean War.
The timing was significant. The visit was on the eve of the 76th anniversary of the Chinese People’s Volunteer Army’s Oct. 25, 1950 first combat against South Korean and U.N. forces in the war, which would rage on for another three years as the Chinese-backed North and U.S. and U.N. backed South fought to what is largely considered to be a stalemate.
The state-run Korean Central News Agency noted that after Kim and the North Korean delegation toured the Memorial Hall of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea, and paid their respects, he told the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference Chairman Wang Huning – the fourth highest ranked official in the Chinese Communist Party – that it was North Korea’s duty to remember the sacrifice of the Chinese army.
“It was a moment to recollect the preciousness of the DPRK-China friendship forged at the cost of blood,” the report attributed him as saying. “We will always remember the history when the excellent sons and daughters of the Chinese people helped our revolution at the cost of their blood and steadily and firmly carry forward the history of the DPRK-China friendship,” Kim said, in the report.
Though international media outlets characterized Kim’s day trip to be an effort to expand trade ties between Pyongyang and Beijing, the visit to the memorial hall was the most important part of the itinerary, Ri Jong Ho, who was once a high-ranking North Korean official but escaped to the South and currently lives in the U.S., told RFA.
“A bridge that stayed closed for twelve years opened only days before Kim crossed it, and on the same day the supreme leader stood before a history his regime has avoided for more than seventy years,” said Ri, questioning whether that was a coincidence or pressure from Beijing, which financed the majority of the new bridge, which lay in a state of near-completion since 2014 before finally opening for trade traffic on Oct. 15.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, left, poses with Wang Huning, China's fourth highest-ranking official, in front of the New Yalu River Bridge that connects Dandong, China with Sinuiju, North Korea, Oct. 24, 2026.
(KCNA via KNS/AFP) There is a consensus among historians that North Korea’s survival in the Korean War was due to Beijing deploying troops to aid Pyongyang, but the story is different inside North Korea.
According to that version of history, the North Korean military under the tactical genius of Kim Jong Un’s grandfather, national founder Kim Il Sung – with only minimal support from China – was able to stave off defeat against an overwhelming force led by the U.S.
This narrative was important from Pyongyang to maintain because it aligns with the country’s founding Juche ideology of self-reliance.
“Pyongyang will present the photographs as proof of an unbreakable friendship. But those inside the Kim system will see something else: the third Kim leader, bowing in public before a history his grandfather and father suppressed,” said Ri.
“Like-minded totalitarians”
Kim’s visit to Dandong is significant because of the timing, but it is more about managing China’s concerns that North Korea is getting too close to Russia, Sydney Seiler, a senior advisor for the Korea Chair at the Washington-based Center for Strategic & International Studies, told RFA.
“Kim is acting with limited confidence, embracing like-minded totalitarian, autocratic … partners such as Russia and China while ignoring the United States, at least for now,” said Seiler. “Kim is working in a ‘safe zone’ between Moscow and Beijing, ensuring that neither side is overly concerned with Pyongyang’s relations with the other, yet still watching to see if and when national interests are threatened.”
He said that at the moment, it is not likely that any moves by Kim and Chinese President Xi Jinping to strengthen their relationship would concern Putin.
“But the opposite is not necessarily true. If Russia’s support to the DPRK enables, empowers, emboldens, and eventually encourages Kim to consider scenarios of even limited use of force toward the ROK, then the PRC will be concerned,” he said, using abbreviations for the official names of South Korea and China. “Kim getting close to the Chinese may be designed to mitigate such concerns.”
But the trip could also be the result of pressure on Kim to finally open the New Yalu River Bridge – and his country, Ri said.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un heading home via the China-North Korea Yalu River Bridge after concluding his visit to China in Dandong, Liaoning province.
(KCNA via KNS/AFP) “I believe Chinese leaders, resentful of the neglected bridge, kept pressing him to open it, and a severe economic crisis left North Korea little choice but to unlock the gate,” he said. “The bridge is open, but I suspect Kim’s fear of opening up, and of the outside information that comes with it, remains deep.”
Ri noted that the bridge had been the vision of Jang Song Thaek, the uncle of Kim Jong Un who supported North Korean economic development through close cooperation with China. Jang in 2009 negotiated to get Beijing to finance the bridge while serving in the regime of Kim Jong Un’s father, Kim Jong Il. Jang’s pro-China views caused him to fall out of favor with the younger Kim and he was executed by firing squad in the early years of his rule following his father’s death.
Message to Washington?
The fact that Kim was able to get into a car and drive to China is intended to point out the lack of effectiveness of sanctions, Hong Min, a senior research fellow at the Seoul-based Korea Institute for National Unification, told RFA.
“The trip implies that ‘one-day shuttle diplomacy’ is possible,” said Hong. “North Korea and China intend to continue close strategic communication regardless of sanctions, and it is a signal that sanctions can effectively be rendered meaningless.”
Because Kim’s visit involved many important officials on both sides, commentators in Seoul and Korea observers raised the possibility that the purpose was for the two countries to coordinate before U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to travel to Shenzhen, China for the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting, and the potential for a summit with Kim while he is in the region.
Ri noted that this was not confirmed and said this kind of meeting would shatter North Korea’s established internal narratives.
“For decades, Pyongyang has preached self-reliance, or juche , and insisted that it bows to no foreign power,” he said. “If its leader must first seek Beijing’s permission before sitting down with an American president, that principle would be hollowed out.”
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, right, shaking hands with Wang Huning, the fourth highest ranked member of the Chinese Communist Party in Dandong, China, Oct. 24, 2026.
(KCNA via KNS/AFP) Ri noted that Kim met with Xi Jinping himself prior to his first summit with Trump in 2018. This time he met only with “China’s No. 4.”
Such a posture would resemble a provincial lord seeking an emperor’s approval,” he said. “An ideology that taught North Koreans for three generations to despise sadae , deference to the powerful, would stand exposed as a slogan.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Transfusion service brings learning
articles.excerpt: A group of SPHRC Kung Yik She Secondary School students recently received a different kind of biology lesson as they…
articles.fullText:
A group of SPHRC Kung Yik She Secondary School students recently received a different kind of biology lesson as they ventured outside of the classroom on a visit to the Yuen Long Blood Donor Centre.

The Hong Kong Red Cross Blood Transfusion Service expanded its “A Biology Class outside of the Classroom” scheme this year. Originally run exclusively at the service’s headquarters, it is now offered at all donor centres, making it much more accessible to school groups.

Real-life settings
Hong Kong Red Cross Blood Transfusion Service Advanced Practice Nurse Lee Wing-sze explained that guided tours, which last an hour, give students the chance to learn in a relaxed and engaging mode.

“As blood-related knowledge is a part of the senior secondary biology curriculum, we integrate these topics into the visit, allowing students to learn within a real-life setting.”

Giving blood
The tour consists of three parts. First, interactive games and information boards are used to introduce basic concepts such as blood types, donor eligibility, and how blood saves lives.

Students then tour the haemoglobin testing area, donation area and blood processing area, learning about overall workflows and the professional equipment involved.

Finally, staff answer questions on the spot to alleviate anxiety and dispel any fears before students make their own decisions on whether to donate blood.

Secondary school student Ryan Yip said that before he experienced the tour, he felt stressed about giving blood.

“I think this whole process is kind of frightening, but after the nurses told me the process is safe and it is all under standard conditions, I think that really comforted me and gave me some confidence to be a voluntary blood donor.”

Another secondary school student, Kelvin To, said he would urge his friends to donate blood after learning about how donations save lives.

Saving lives
The service’s Head of Blood Collection & Donor Recruitment Department Dr Jacky Kong said that establishing a solid foundation of blood-related knowledge is crucial to encouraging teenagers to become blood donors in the long run.

“We believe that interaction with our staff and blood donors is very important for them to be exposed to why blood donation is important for the public.”

The service reaches out to secondary schools across Hong Kong and, to date, has arranged talks or donor centre visits for more than 60 schools in the current academic year.

SPHRC Kung Yik She Secondary School Principal Liu Siu-lin said she fully supports the lessons the service provides as they allow students to witness first-hand how blood is processed and transformed into life-saving products.

“This unique lesson shows that science is not just about cold data, but about saving lives.”

articles.title: CS attends talent event in Dongguan
articles.excerpt: Chief Secretary Chan Kwok-ki today attended an opening ceremony for two initiatives promoting the Greater Bay Area (GBA) in Dongguan…
articles.fullText:
Chief Secretary Chan Kwok-ki today attended an opening ceremony for two initiatives promoting the Greater Bay Area (GBA) in Dongguan – namely the fourth GBA High-quality Talent Development Conference and the third GBA Doctoral and Postdoctoral Innovation and Entrepreneurship Competition.

Addressing the ceremony, he said Hong Kong will continue to attract the talent required for its own and the country's development, and will work with other GBA cities to advance the alignment of rules and mechanisms that facilitate the flow of talent within the area.

Mr Chan outlined that Hong Kong's First Five-Year Plan proactively aligns with the National 15th Five-Year Plan and promotes the integrated development of education, technology and talent. He added that the Northern Metropolis University Town will closely connect Hong Kong's strengths in basic research and internationalised education with both the innovation and technology (I&T) and talent resources of the broader GBA.

After the ceremony, Mr Chan and Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun toured the exhibition hall and visited the Hong Kong Talent Engage booth.

Yesterday, Mr Chan and his delegation visited a key I&T enterprise in Dongguan to better understand the local model of fostering co-operation between the spheres of scientific research, innovation, and talent development. They subsequently toured the City University of Hong Kong (Dongguan) to learn about synergies between Hong Kong and Dongguan in higher education and talent cultivation, and to explore ways of strengthening complementarity between the two places.

Mr Chan and Mr Sun concluded their visit to Dongguan this morning and returned to Hong Kong in the afternoon.

articles.title: Live K-pop show makes South Korea more real to former North Korean arts troupe singer
articles.excerpt: “I really am in the South now,” said Cho Mi-young - at her first K-pop show - 22 years after…
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
A white tiger entered the courtyard outside the National Museum in Seoul. He mugged for the camera and darted up the steps. At the top were the six members of BOYNEXTDOOR, wearing quasi-traditional outfits that mixed elements of hanbok with modern formal wear and a tinge of “bad boy” biker gear.
As they danced in unison and sang the opening lines of their hit single “Animal,” the crowd went wild.
Sitting in the audience was Cho Mi-young – born in Chongjin, North Korea – who arrived with her family in the South in 2004.
Mi-young can’t contain herself. “You’re so amazing!” she cries out, as the monitors show the young men dominating the courtyard with their precise dance moves.
Cho is in the audience at an episode of KBS Music Bank, a Friday night K-pop showcase program with all the latest acts. It has been the start of the K-pop weekend for most of its 28-year runtime. Surprisingly, it’s her first time ever seeing a live K-pop performance in person after 22 years in the South.
Tickets to studio tapings of KBS Music Bank are hard to come by. Fans either have to know someone, know someone who knows someone, or enter the ticket lottery. The episode she’s watching on Oct. 16 is special - it’s a live broadcast and the biggest boy bands, girl bands, and boy-girl bands are plying their craft on an outdoor stage on the grounds of the National Museum of Korea, which the show’s special intro vignette called the “beating heart of Korean culture.”
When the opening act was finished, the show’s hosts began introducing this week’s lineup, as Cho and the rest of the audience settled in. Many more K-pop groups and solo artists would take the stage in front of them on a night they would likely all remember forever.
“I’ve seen it a lot on TV, but today is the first time I’ve seen it with my own eyes,” Cho told Radio Free Asia. “Seeing such beautiful and handsome people dancing and singing right in front of me, moving like that, is absolutely mesmerizing.”
Cho is no stranger to music, or to the stage. In North Korea she had been a vocalist for a state-run provincial arts troupe. After settling in the South, Cho was a fixture in Seoul’s burgeoning musical theater scene and she toured as an accordion player. She later transitioned into broadcasting, at one point even co-hosting the RFA Korean webseries “ Northboy Northgirl .”
At present, she runs a content production company and maintains an active presence both online and in traditional media.
Cho Mi-young watches a live broadcast of KBS Music Bank at the National Museum of Korea in Seoul, Oct. 16, 2026.
(RFA) But today, she’s just a fangirl in a sea of other diehards, most of whom are screaming the names of the idols on stage.
Music in isolation
